Petition of A Petition of the Booksellers and Printers of the

&c°ref*eftin Cities of London and Wevvhofe Names are there-

the"Duty on unto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read;

Paper- ' Setting forth. That the Petitioners have ever been willing cheerfully to bear their Proportion, in common with the rest of His Majesty's Subjects, towards the Expences of the State, but they humbly beg Leave to represent to the House, that the additional Duty imposed upon Printing Paper and Milled Board, during the last Session of Parliament, has greatly affected the Trades of printing and felling Books, and has injured the Interests of the Petitioners, inso much that if it be not repealed, it must infallibly tend to the Destruction of a Trade very beneficial and important to the Country, namely, that of printing, felling, and exporting Books, and consequently occasion a Diminution in the Receipt of the public Revenue; and that this Tax is peculiarly oppressive upon the Petitioners as a trading Body, and falls directly and wholly upon their Capitals, and but slowly upon the Public at large, because, in printing an Edition of any Book, they are under the Necessity of immediately purchasing and using the Whole of the Paper, the Duty on which has been previously paid, notwithstanding the Edition may be many Years upon Sale, or may never be fold; and they beg Leave to explain to the House, that, in order to fell Books at a moderate Price, and to lay upon each Copy as small a Proportion as possible of the heavy Expence of the Copyright, and of the first setting up of the Press, they are always obliged to print a much larger Number of Copies than can be sold for a considerable Time, and they are thus, from this peculiar Feature attending the Production of Books, under the Necessity of paying for heavy Stocks of printed Paper before a Angle Specimen of the manufactured Article can be produced for Sale; whereas the Generality of Manufacturers are exempted from this expensive Necessity, as they can manufacture their Articles at such Times, and.in such Proportions, as the Demand may require; and that, to diminish the ruinous Effects of the present high Price of Paper, and to prevent the Increase of their expensive Stocks, the Petitioners have, in some Instances, forborne to re-print new Editions of meritorious Works, and have also, in other Instances, been induced to print much smaller Editions of Books than was formerly their Practice, in consequence of which* the Expence of the Copyright, and of the first setting up of the Press, being necessarily laid upon a smaller Number, the separate Copies have unavoidably been raised in their Price; it has, however, been found, that the consequent Advance in the Price of Books to the Public has greatly diminished their Sale; the Petitioners, therefore, find no adequate Resource in their own Means, and are compelled to apply to the House for Relief; and that the Petitioners are aware that it might have been expected they would have found Relief in the Application of various new Inventions in the Manufacture of Paper, which have been proposed to the Public, and some cf which have received the Sanction of the Legislature; but not any of these Inventions have hitherto enabled their Conductors and Proprietors to offer their Paper in a State suitable to print Books upon, at a Price which promises to lessen the Grievance above dated; and that the Petitioners are especially called upon at this Time to pray for Relief, because they have recently found that Editions of all the belt and most favourite English Authors have been printed, and are now printing, in various Sizes, at Berlin, Bajle, burgh, Paris, Philadelphia, and other Cities in

Europe and America, and, as some of these foreign Editions are offered for Sale at One-Half of the Price at which the same Books can be printed and sold at a very Vo h.si'

moderate Profit by the Petitioners, they are threatened with the Loss of their Export Trade to America and to the Et<ropean Continent especially, and to other Parts of the World; since, by Means of foreign Yeifels from the Ports on both Sides of the Atlantic, the cheap foreign Editions of English Books are, with Facility, transported to the British and other European Settlements in Acts and the West Indies-, and that, as it may be alledged that the Petitioners, in their Export Trade, have a Relief in the Drawback of Four-Fifths, or Two-pence per Pound Weight upon printed Books exported, they feel it incumbent upon them to observe, that this Relief is inadequate, and does not enable the Petitioners to meet foreign Competitors in foreign Markets; because the full Drawback actually received seldom amounts to more than One-Third of the Duty, and upon the whole Exports not to One-Tenth, because not any of the additional Advance consequent upon the new Duty is drawn back; because not any of the Advance on Printing* which has occurred within the Two last Years, is drawn back; and because every other Expence attending the Production of Books is much higher in Britain

than in other Parts of the World; and that, although in consequence of the Peace, the raw Material is lower in Price, and Paper in some Degree cheaper, yet the Reduction has not been so great, nor is it likely to be so great, as to enable the Petitioners to maintain the Export Trade in Books, inasmuch as the Price of the raw Material is fluctuating, while the Duty remains a permanent Charge upon which the Manufacturer and Stationer put as permanent a Profit; and that the Petitioners are-convinced, that the injurious Tendency of this Tax will operate nearly as a Prohibition of every new Literary Speculation, and consequently that the Revenue, instead of being benefited by the new Duty, will eventually sustain a considerable Injury; whereas, if the last Duty upon Printing Papers (strictly so called) Copper-plate Papers, and Milled Boards, be repealed, it appears to the Petitioners that the increased Demand for printed Books which would naturally follow a Reduction of their Price* would in a great Measure compensate, by an increased Demand for Printing Papers* this small Deduction from the Revenue; and that, by the Operation of this Tax* an important Branch of Trade is thus in a great Measure diverted from the Country, the Petitioners are restrained from rilking their Capitals, in the Uncertainty of meeting with an adequate Return, many Thousands of British Subjects, engaged in the various Branches of Paper Making, Printing, Bookselling, Engraving, and Bookbinding, in Danger of being deprived of Subsistence, the Progress of Education is impeded, the Extension of Knowledge and Literature* manifestly diminished, and the national Genius discouraged and depressed; and that the Petitioners are prepared to prove the various Allegations above stated, if thought necessary, which they beg Leave to submit to the Consideration of the House:

And therefore praying for such Relief as to the Wisdom of the House shall appear to be expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, the said Acts were read: — And,

Mr. Thomas Ridding being examined, said, That the Trustees of the South District, together with those of the North District of the Southampton Road, were authorized, by the said Act of the 31st Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, to erect Gates or Turnpikes between the City of Winchester and the Town and County of the Town of Southampton, except within Three Miles of Bar Gate, in the said Town and County, and to take Tolls thereat; that, by the said Act of the 20th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the said Road from Winchester to Southampton was divided into Two Districts, and the Clause restricting the Erection of a Gate nearer Bar Gate, in the Town and County of the Town of Southampton, than Three Miles, was repealed, so that the Trustees of the South District were then empowered to erect Gates or Turnpikes across any Part of that District, and to take certain Tolls thereat; and that, by virtue of the said several Acts of Parliament, considerable Sums of Money have been borrowed upon the Credit of the Tolls to be ccllefted at the Gate* erected, or to be erected, under the Powers of the said Acts. — And the Witness being further examined, said. That, by the Act of the 41st "Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Trustees of the South District are reflrifted from taking any Toll at any Gate or Turnpike which should thereafter be erected within 800 Yards of Bar Gate, in the Town and County of the Town of Southampton, for any longer Term than Three succeeding Calendar Months, unless it should appear that the Money collected at all the Gates erected within the said South District should be inl'ufficient to enable the said Trustees to keep the said Road in Repair, and in that same only they are empowered to take Tolls in the luceeeding Year, for any Period not exceeding Four succeeding Months; by which Restriction the Security of the several Creditors upon the said Road is conltder-ably diminished. — And being further examined, he said. That under the said Act of the 41st Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Company of Proprietors of Northam Bridge and Roads claim an Exemption from Toll for all Cattie and Carriages passing and re-passing Northam Bridge and Roads to and from the Town of Southampton, and that, if such Exemption should be construed as having been granted by the said Act, the same will be very injurious to the said District of Road, and will also further diminish the Tolls to be collected thereon; and that the said Trustees are, by the last mentioned Act, empowered to borrow, and take up at Interest, over and above the Sum then due and owing, any further Sum of Money not exceeding £.3,000, and they have given Notice of their Intention to borrow more Money upon the Credit of the said Tolls, but that the same cannot be obtained without the said restrictive Clause is repealed. — And the Witness added, That the said District of the Southampton Road is in a very bad Condition, and cannot be put in a proper State of Repair, unless the Powers of the said several Acts are altered, amended, and enlarged; and that it would be highly beneftcial to the Public in general, and to the Inhabitants of Southampton, wood, and Swathling, in particular, that the Road leading from the East Side of the South District of the Southampton Road, near Belle Vue, in the Parish of Saints, in the Town and County of the Town of Southampton, through Rockftone Lane, in the Parish of Saint Mary, in the said Town and County of the Town of Southampton, and Portswood, in the Parish of South Stone-ham, partly within the Liberties of the said Town and County of the Town of Southampton, and partly within the County of Southampton, to the Bridge over the River at Swathling, in the said Parish of South Stoneham, in the County of Southampton, should be made a Part of the South District of the Southampton Road.

A Petition of sundry Noblemen, Gentlemen, and Veterinary others, Subscribers to an Institution called The -nary College, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth. That, in pursuance of the Plan Hated to the House in a Petition by them presented on the 6th of February 1795, their Exertions have been continued to carry into Effect the several beneficial Purposes proposed to be derived from the Establishment of a College for the Study and Practice of Veterinary Science; that, for the general Benefit of the Proprietors of Horses, and other valuable Cattle, they have Pleasure in Hating, that One hundred and One Pupils have passed Examination at the said College, many of whom are now settled in different Towns of the Kingdom, and are practising the Knowledge they have acquired, to the great Advantage of the Public; and it is with particular Satisfaction the Petitioners are enabled to (late, that the Importance of the Institution having been taken into Consideration by His Royal Highness the Commander in Chief, the Propriety of appointing Persons educated at the College to be Veterinary Surgeons in the several Regiments of Cavalry has been determined on, in pursuance of a Report from a Board of General Officers, to whom the Subject had been referred; and that, in consequence of such Decision, Thirty-four Pupils, whose Education has been completed, are engaged in the Service of the Army, and Twenty-five other Pupils are now pursuing their Studies at the College, several of them intending to fill limilar Situations as soon as they shall be deemed duly qualified, each of

them

them being subject to the same rigorous Examination Of the Medical Committee, and to be certified in the same Manner as has hitherto been practised in respect of the other Pupils of the College; a;id the Petitioners further state, that desirous of rendering, to the utmost of their Power, their Institution advantageous to the public Service, the Colonels of the different Cavalry Regiments have been invited to fend each a Farrier to . the College, in order to his being taught the Structure, Economy, and different Diseases of the Horse's Foot, and instructed in a Mode of Shoeing, tending very materially to its Preservation; and that many Army Farriers have been consequently admitted into the College for Instruction in that particular Part of Veterinary Knowledge; and that the College continues under the Direction of the Professor, Mr. , a Gentleman

of Talents and Skill, and who, by many useful and important Discoveries in the Science, has, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, fully justified the Expectations formed of its Improvement from his Exertions; and that the Petitioners have already Rated to the House the Difficulties which have occurred in the Execution of their Plan, and particularly from the embarrassed State of their Finances; and though the Aid l'o liberally granted by Parliament, has, in a great Degree, alleviated their Difficulties, it has yet proved inadequate to remove thenventirelv, notwithstanding the Petitioners have, with the utmost Frugality, reduced their Annual Expenditure much within the Estimate of the Committee of the House, to whom the former Petition was referred, and within those Limits to which they are still of Opinion it would be proper to extend it, in order that the Public may derive the full Benefit of such an Establishment, the Petitioners have again, with Regret, to state, that (under the heavy Prefl'ure of Debt, of which an Account is before the House) without further Aid from Parliament, it will be impossible to bring to Perfection an Establishment which, from the Advantages accruing from the more skilful Care of so important a Branch of public Property as the Horses , of the Army, is become, more than ever, an Object of National Importance: And therefore praying, That they may have such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Day of June, in the 7th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King Charles the Second, a Lighthouse was established at Tinmouth, in the County of Northumberland, for the Accommodation of Ships and Vessels coming into and going out of the Harbour and Port of 'Tinmouth, which Lighthouse, and the Ground and Soil whereon the same was situate, was thereby veiled in Edward Villiers(afterwards Sir Knight) his Heirs and Assigns, who were authorized to take the Sum of 12 d.for every Veil'd passing by the said Lighthouse, and belonging or trading to the Ports of Newcastle and Sunderland, and 35. for every Ship of, or belonging to, any Foreigner or Stranger coming or passing by the said Lighthouse; the said Edward Villiers, his Heirs and Assigns, yielding and paying the refore Yearly to the said King, his Heirs and Successors, such Rent as therein mentioned; and that the Petitioner, as Nephew of , Widow of Henry

Villiers, Grandson of the said Patentee Sir Edward Villiers, is now become seised of the said Lighthouse and Premises; and that the Maficr, Wardens, and Assistants of the Corporation of Trinity of

Newcastle upon Tyne, and a great Number of Merchants,

Traders, Owners, and Mailers of Ships, and others, interested in the Trade and Navigation of the Ports of Newcastle upon Tyne and Sunderland, and the Parts adjacent, taking into Consideration the present State of the said Tinmouth Lighthouse and Light, and the great Benefit which would result to the Navigation of the said Ports of Newcastle and Sunderland, and the Parts adjacent, if the said Lighthouse should be altered by taking down a Part thereof, and erecting a Copper Lighthouse Lanthorn, and by substituting for the present Coal Light, an Oil Light, on the improved Principle of Mr. George Robinson, by Patent Lamps, and high polished Silver plated Refledlors, with a revolving Machine, according to a Plan and Estimate lately made for the Purpose by the said George Robinson, have requested the Petitioner, as present Proprietor of the said Lighthouse and Light, to cause the said Lighthouse and Light to be altered accordingly; and, in Consideration of the Colls and E# pences which the Petitioner will thereby necessarily incur, and of the increased annual Expence which will attend the keeping, maintaining, and managing of the said Lighthouse and Light, in a proper Manner, according to the said Alteration and Improvement, have signified their full Consent to having certain additional Light Duties granted; and that the Petitioner is willing to cause the said Lighthouse and Light to be altered, improved, and maintained, in Manner before-mentioned, upon the Terms of having such additional Light Duties granted, as have been so consented to by the several Penons aforesaidj and that such Alteration and Improvement in the said Lighthouse and Light as aforesaid, may be of great public Utility, by contributing to the Safety and Preservation of the Lives, Ships, and Goods of His Majesty's Subjects and others, navigating and passing by the said Lighthouse and Light: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, and for raising a competent Sum of Money, by way of Mortgage, of the said Lighthouse, to defray the necessary Costs and Charges thereto relating.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That, from the extensive Population of the Cities of London and Westminsterand Liberties thereof, and from the

Various Trades exercised, and different Manufactures carried on therein, great Quantities of Coals are daily Con-fumed, for the constant Supply of which, Ships frequenting the Port of London employed in the Coal Trade are very numerous; and that it is of the utmost Consequence to the very Existence of fevera1 of the said Trades and Manufactures, in which the Consumption of Fuel must of Necessity be very great, that such Fuel should be obtained at as reasonable a Hate as possible; and that it would tend greatly to reduce the present very high Price of Coals (by preventing, in a considerable Degree* illicit Practices and Combinations in the Coal Trade in the Port of London, having for their Object the railing of the Price to the Consumer) if a Market, under certain Rules and Restrictions, was established for the Sale of all Coals brought into the River 'Thames, by means of which the Quantity and Descriptions of Coals brought in each and every Vessel, and the Price at which the same were fold, might be generally known, and if certain other Regulations were made in the Vend of Coals brought into the Port of London: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, by such Ways and Means as to the House shall seem meet.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the 17 th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for " repealing the Eleventh Rule in the Book of Rates, to " far as the same relates to making any Allowance upon " the Importation of damaged Currants and Raisins, and " for making the Importer of such Goods an Abatement " in the Duties in Lieu thereof, and for explaining the rt laid Rule with respect to such Allowance for Damage " on other Goods, and to permit the Exportation of " Tobacco Pipe Clay from this Kingdom to the " Sugar Colonies or Plantations in the West Indies, for a " limited Time," as permits the Exportation of Tobacco Pipe Clay from this Kingdom to the British Sugar Colonies or Plantations in the West Indies, which was to continue in Force until the 24th Day of June 1779, and from thence to the End of the then next Sdlion of Parliament, and which, by several subsequent Acts, was further continued until the 24th Day of June 1802, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That lb much of an Act, made in the 8th Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, "An Act for " giving further Encouragement for the Importation of " Naval Stores, and for other Purposes therein mentioned," as relates to the Importation of Wood and Timber, and of the Goods commonly called Lumber, therein part icularly enumerated, from any of His Majesty's British Plantations or Colonies in America, free from all Customs and Impositions whatsoever, which was to be in Force for Twenty-one Years from the 24th Day of June 1722, and which by several subsequent Acts was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1802, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee; That an Act, made in the 38 th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for regulating the " Payment, until Two Months after the Commencement " of the next Session of Parliament after the End of the " present War, of the Duties on Cinnamon, Cloves, Nutmegs, and Mace, and for granting to His Majesty - " additional Duties thereon," is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That fe> much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for allowing, until the First " Day of AugustOne thousand Eight hundred and Two,

" the Importation of certain Fish from Newfoundland " and the Coast of Labrador, and for granting a Bounty

" thereon," as relates to the permitting-the Importation of certain Fish from Newfoundland and the Coast of Labrador, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 35th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty,- intituled, "An Act for allowing, for a " limited Time, the Importation of Goods from India " and China, and other Parts within the Limits of the " exclusive Trade of the East India Company, in Ships " not of British-built, nor registered as such, and for the

" Exportation of Goods from Great Britain by the same " Ships, under certain Restrictions," which was to continue in Force during the Continuance of the present War, and for Eighteen Months after the Conclusion thereof, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for reviving, continuing until the " Twentieth Day of May One thousand Eight hundred " and Two, and amending an Act, made in the Thirtyninth and Fortieth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to repeal the Duties on Sugar " and Cofee exported, granted by an Act, passed in the

Petition. was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Port of Southampton is a very ancient one, from which, of late Years, a considerable Trade and Commerce has been carried on to Foreign Parts as well as Coallwile, and from the Situation of which, and other concurring Circumstances, is capable of being greatly improved, and rendered very commodious, by a Bason and Wet Docks being conftrafted, capable of receiving and harbouring a considerable Number of Ships, much larger than can now lie with Safety at the Quays to be laden or unladen, which would tend to the Increase of Navigation, and Improvement of Trade, within the said Town and Port, and eventually increase the Commerce and Navigation of the Kingdom; and that the Petitioners are entitled, by virtue of several Charters, to certain exclusive Privileges, and also to divers Customs, Duties, and Payments, from all Persons trading to or from the said Port, which Payments will not be sufficient to carry the intended Plans into Execution; and that the Petitioners are willing and desirous to give up such exclusive Rights, as well as that the present Wharfage Dues payable to them should be regulated, and that a new Book of Rates should be made, to establish the Harbour Dues to be paid by them in their private Capacities, as well as by all other Persons trading to or from the said Port, for the Purpose of carrying Rich Improvements and Alterations into Execution; and that the Petitioners, as well as the Provost and Scholars of the Queen sCollege in the University of Oxford, Warden of the Hospital of God's Hoitfe in the Town of Southampton, the Warden and Scholars Clerks of Mary College, Winchester, near Winchester, and the lteftors or Vicars of the several Parishes of Holy Rhood, Saint Michael, Saint John, and Saint Lawrence, in the said Town of Southamp-

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the 16th and 17 th Years of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for making the said River navigable; and allb Two other Acts, passed in the 17th and 35th Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, to alter and amend the said Act, were read: — And,

Mr. Alexander Westlake. Clerk and Agent to the Petitioners, being examined, laid, That the Petitioners are the lole Proprietors of the said River, which is navigated on very different Principles to almost any other in the Kingdom, the Proprietors being obliged, by the Acts that have regulated the Navigation thereof, to provide Barges, and maintain Horses, Labourers, and Drivers, for conveying Goods on the said River, at certain Rates, for the whole Length of the Navigation: That if every Person that thought proper was permitted to navigate on the said River, paying Rates of Tonnage, it would produce Competition, and the City of PVinchester, and Places adjacent, would be supplied with Coals and other Commodities at a much cheaper Rate than they are, or can be, under the present System: — Then,

Mr. Edward Pyott ll'ijllake being examined, confirmed the above Evidence. — And,

Mr. Alexander Westlake, being again examined, produced to Your Committee, an Account of the Receipt and Expenditure of the said Proprietors for the Three last Years; by which it appeared that they had received the Sum of £.6,929. is. 3d. and had expended Vol. 57.

£.6,968. i8r. o,\d. being a Lois of £.39. 16 in that Period. — Then, the Conveyance of the said River to the Petitioners was produced to Your Committee; by which it appeared, that they had paid a large Sum of Money for the Purchase thereof, besides being engaged for the Payment of a considerable Sum of Money charged on the said Navigation. — And the Witness, being further examined, said, That the River was in a very bad State when purchased by the present Proprietors, the Locks and Banks being very much out of Repair: That it will require at leall £. 2,coo to put them into a complete State of Reparation, which, with the Purchase Money, Charges on the Navigation, and Money already expended by the Proprietors, make a Capital of more than £. 20,000; and he conceives it to be impossible for the Proprietors to derive any Advantage from the River under the present System. — And the Witness added, That a Canal is now making from the said River to Southampton, which, it is expected, will

be completed in the Course of the present Year, on which Goods are to be conveyed on paying a Tonnage Duty, and if the like Mode was to be adopted on the River Itchin, the same Method of charging for the Conveyance of Goods and Merchandize w'ould operate the whole Way from Southampton to much to

the Convenience of Persons trading to and from those Places.

Setting fortl), That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has for a long Series of Years been carried on by a Society of Merchants, incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on this Trade with Safety, and protect His Majesty's Subjects in the Dominions, it has

been found necessary that an Ambassador or Public Mini (ter should be lent from England to reside at Constantinople, and that Consuls, Vice Consuls, with proper Officers and Servants, should be established in the other Parts of Turkey where British Subjects reside, and where the English Merchants carry on Trade, the whole Expence of which has been borne by the Company, which, together with other Expences incident to carrying on the Trade, have of late Years amounted to about 80,000 per Annum; and that the Petitioners feel it incumbent on them to represent that the House, which has always been appropriated for the Reception of His Majesty's Ambassador at the Porte, is fallen to Decay, and it will be necessary to cause a new one to be built, in case it should be thought expedient to provide*a permanent Residence for a Public Officer of so much Consequence, a Measure which muffc be left to the Wisdom of Parliament, and, if adopted, will necessarily be attended with considerable Expence; that, in Addition to the ordi-naiy (landing Expences of the Company, the Petitioners are likely to be put to a heavy Charge in re-building the Consulary House at Smyrna, destroyed by the melancholy Fire which happened in the Year 1797, in consequence of a popular Tumult; and that the Petitioners acknowledge with Gratitude the Grants they have frequently received from Parliament; but they are fenlible they should not discharge the Duty imposed on them by their Charter, nor the Justice which they owe to the Public (for whom they consider themselves as Trustees) if they did not declare their present Inability to defray so heavy a Charge, and to support their Establishments in Turkey, without the Assistance of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as may be thought necclfaty and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.

A Petition of His Majesty's Justices of the Peace in and for the County Palatine of assembled at

a Special Setfion, held at Proton, in and for the said County, the 19th Day of November 1801, pursuant to the Statute, was prefen ted to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Inhabitants of the said County have of late Years been greatly opprefi'ed, and put to great Expence, by having lately had the Repairs of ineffectual Bridges, heretofore unknown, thrown upon them, and which were built by Subscription, and otherwise, without any Authority from the County, and merely for the private Purposes of Individuals, but which, by some late Determinations, the County becomes obliged to re-build and support, to an incalculable Expence and Increase of the public Burthens of the County, and which Grievance is still increasing; and that, previous to the Year 1784, the said Inhabitants only repaired Six County Bridges, the others being repaired by the Hundreds, Parishes, Townships, and other Districts, within the said County , but that since the 1 aft-mentioned Period, the Repairs of Five additional Bridges have been added thereto; and that the Petitioners are desirous that the Public should be accommodated with Bridges where they are really wanted, on proper Conditions, but submit, that all new Bridges, which are afterwards to be upheld and supported at the Expence of the County, should be built with the Knowledge, Approbation, and by the Authority of the Magistrates of the County: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to amend, and render more effectual, the Laws respecting County Bridges, lb far as the same relate to the County Palatine of Lancaster, and to effectuate the Purposes aforesaid.

and that the said Low Grounds and Carrs now are, and for some Years pall have been, subject to be overflowed with Water, so as to be wholly unfit for the Purposes of Agriculture, to the great Damage and Loss of the Owners and Occupiers thereof, and of the Public; and that there arc very considerable Quantities of Land within the said several Parishes, Townships, and Places, amounting to a,000 Acres and upwards, capable of receiving Benefit from the said Drainage, over and above the Low Grounds and Carrs which are now included in the said Act; and that the Drainage of all the said Low Grounds and Carrs, and other Lands, is capable of being made complete and effectual by opening a certain ancient Drain called Hall Bridge Drain, and discharging the Waters of certain of the said Parishes, Townships, and Places, through the said ancient Drain called Hall Bridge Drain, into the River Humber,

thence, by Stranraer, to the Confines of the County of Ayr, near the Cairn of Lochryan, being one of the great Communications between Engl Scotland, and Ireland, is in bad Repair, and cannot be properly amended, and kept in Repair* unless Tolls are allowed to be levied thereon, and other Powers are given; and that the Laws how subsisting for the'making of Roads and building Bridges, and repairing the fame, have been found ineffectual in the said County of Wigtown to make and maintain the Roads through the same generally, and other and further Powers are necessary in order to carry the Purposes of the said Laws into Execution; and it is attended with Difficulty to make effectual, and properly to apply, the Statute Work in the said County; and that a reasonable Composition in Money, in Lieu of actual Labour, is in many Places found to be more useful and effectual for the Purpose of making and repairing the Roads, as well as more easy and convenient for the Persons liable in Statute Service than the actual Performance; and it would therefore be of Advantage to the said County of Wigtown to convert the Statute Services

into Money, and to ascertain the Rates thereof, and the Mode of levying the lame, and to authorize an additional Assessment than that at present allowed to be imposed on the Heritors of Lands, and other Persons, in the said County, for making Highways and Bridges through the same: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes before-mentioned, with such Powers, and under such Provisions, as to the House may. seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof , and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Mr. Lifbinglon reported from the Committee, to whem the Petition of the Planters, Merchants, and others, trading to, and connected with, the Iliar.ds of Grenada and Saint Vincent, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; vie.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. 'Thomas Coles, Sugar Broker, being examined, said. That Sugar at present is very unsaleable, except at a low

Vol. 57.

Price; that the Price has declined for these Eighteen Months pall, particularly since the Signature of the Preliminaries of Peace; that the Average Price of Grenada Sugar is from 48/. to 62 s. per Hundred Weight; that the Average Charges were from 38 s. to 40 per Cwt.; that Sugar is at present full Twenty per Cent, lower than the Average Price during the War; and that the high Prices of Sugar were previous to the Year 1798, when the Islands of Grenada and Saint Vincent were unproductive on account of the Insurrections. — The Witness all'o stated. That Sugars were very low last Year, and that they arc at present full Seven Shillings Cwt. lower than last Year; and that all the Sugars at present on Hand were imported subject to the War Charges: — And,

Mr. William Arnold, of the Island of Grenada (not interested in the Subject before Your Committee) said. That hc^had resided in Grenada for near Thirty Years, and, fr<5m his general Knowledge and Experience, the Expence of cultivating Sugar was on an Average about £.10 perHogfhead of 12 Cwt. exchiiive of the Rum,

which arises from the Supplies sent out from Europe, and Bills drawn from the Island for Expences which the Rum was inadequate to defray; that he considered the Expences of last Year to have exceeded the Average of preceding Years, from the high Price of Provisions, Materials, and Supplies of all Sorts; that, from the present Price of Sugar, after deducing the Charges and Expences, nothing would remain for the Planter, who would inevitably be brought into Debt; that the Supplies of Stores from Europe w$re equal to £.5 per Hogshead on the Cultivation of each Estate, exclusive of Provisions for the Negroes, and other Articles provided in the Island. — Then,

Mr. Thomas Marsham, Secretary to the Commissioners for iiluing Exchequer Bills to the Sufferers by the Infur-rections in the Islands of Grenada and Saint Vincent, being examined, said, That the Sum remaining due from the Merchants, Planters, and others of Grenada and Saint Vincent, by public Loan, is amply secured to the Satisfaction of the Commissioners, and that it bears an Interest of Five per Cent.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

A petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of Kllates, and nfident within the Township of Ponfefraft, and an adjoining Township called in the West

Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That about the Beginning of the Infl Century several charitable and well-disposed Persons raised considerable Sums of Money by Subscription, and otherwise, which were laid out in Housing and Lands, the Rents and Profits whereof have been applied towards the cloathing and instructing of Male and Female Children within the said Townships, and the Institution has been under the Direction of certain Persons who have been Subscribers of One Guinea or more Annually; but.it is not certainly known in whom the legal Lftnte in the said real Property is vested, nor are there any known Rules or Orders for the Management of the said Institution; and that, by the Alteration of Times, the said real Property is now become of great Value, although, for the Reasons before mentioned, the same is enjoyed by Individuals ' at infuior Rents, and the Advantages arifrng from it are comparatively small; but if proper Trustees were appointed, the said Property was disposed of, and the

Money arising therefrom Converted and applied to the greatest Advantage, and if Regulations were made for the due Management of the said Institution, the Benefits arising from it to the Inhabitants of the said Townships . would be greatly increased and advanced; and that there are also, within the said Townships of Pontefract and Tanjhelf, several Hospitals, to which a considerable

Property in Housing, Lands, and Rents appertain; and there are other Properties in Housing, Lands, and Rents, which belong to the Poor of the said several Townships at large, which Properties being for the most Part also got into the Hands of Individuals at Rents greatly below their Value, the Inhabitants are deprived of great Part of the Profits which might be made thereof; but if the same were also disposed of, and the Money arising therefrom applied to the greatest Advantage, great Benefit would accrue to the said Hospitals and Inhabitants, and the Poor Rates (which are extravagantly high) would be reduced; and that, besides the several Advantages above specified, the Properties comprized in the above Descriptions have been many Years in Mortmain, and their being disposed of would furnish many Conveniences to divers Persons who would give advanced Prices for the Purchase thereof: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for eflefting the several Purposes above-mentioned, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names care thereunto subscribed, being Persons professing the Jewtfb Religion, and denominated German , on Behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and' read; Setting forth. That within the last Fifty Years the Number of Jews resident in England have considerably increased, a very great Proportion of whom are in very indigent Circumstances; and that, although the Jewish Poor have an equal Right with other Members of the Community to Parochial Relief when in Distress; yet the peculiar Circumstances of their religious Rites and Diet completely shut them out of all Places established for the Relief of the Poor, and the same Cause deprives them (when afflicted with Sickness, or maimed by any Accident) of the Benefit to be derived from medical Aid administered in the different Hospitals in this Metropolis, and prevents the Children of Jews from being bound to mechanical and many other Employments, by which they might be enabled to become useful Members of Society; and that, in the present State of the Class of the Jewish Nation, of whom the Petitioners form a Part, there is no Asylum to which the aged and infirm can resort for Succour and Protection when Debility or Disease assail them, nor any Place for the Education and Maintenance of the Infant Poor; and that the Relief afforded from the Synagogues is, under the present Circumstances, very inadequate; and , for Want of proper Regulations, is inefficiently applied; and that the Petitioners conceive it would be highly advantageous to the Persons denominated German Jews, residing in the City of London and the Bills of Mortality, including Saint Pancras and , if Power

was given to regulate and maintain their Poor, and to promote Industry, and a Knowledge of useful and productive Labour among them, and thereby render them more useful Members of Society than they are, or can be, under their present peculiar Circumstances: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations as the House shall think proper and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Dr. Smyth's A Petition of James Carmichael Smyth, M. D. being rf vmi on 3 offered to be presented to the House;

Accoimt°of Mr. Bragge (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted Public the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of Sttvues. the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Stating certain Fadts and Circumstances relative to a Discovery made by the Petitioner respecting the Vapour of the Nitrous Acid, and that it has been proved by Experiment to be one of the most powerful Means of destroying Contagion, whilst, at the same Time, when diffused in any Quantity in the common Atmosphere, it is shewn to be perfectly respirable, and attended neither with Danger nor Inconvenience, and that it is, perhaps, the only Mineral Acid that can be used with Safety in the Apartments of the Sick, and in all Situations where People are necessarily present; that this House were pleated to present an Address to His Majesty in Favour of the Petitioner, on account of his Attendance upon the Spanij Prisoners at Winchcsler; and that the Petitioner has, on various Occasions, been applied to by the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, and other Public Boards, for his Assistance in Cafes of Contagion existing in the Fleet and public Hospitals, and that his Endeavours have been crowned with Success, not only in this Country, but also on the Continent of Europe-, and that the Petitioner, by devoting so much of his Time to an Object of public Utility, has sacrificed private to public Advantage, and that, in so doing, he has suffered not the Loss of Time only, but of Health and Fortune; and that the Petitioner, for all his Labours, has as yet received no Recompence or Reward; but he looks up to the Justice of the House: And therefore praying the House to take his same into Consideration, and to grant him such Reward for his Services to the Public, and Loss of Time aforesaid, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Wilberforce, Mr. Bragge, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morffing, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Bragge (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth. That, in the 2d Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the said Trustees represented to Parliament, that the Sum allowed them for the Establishment and Support of the said Museum was reduced to a Capital of £. 30,000 Reduced Bank Annuities, the Dividend of which, amounting to £.900, was, notwithstanding their utmost Attention to the forming their Establishment with Frugality, greatly insufficient for that Purpose; upon which Representation they have, at sundry Times, obtained from the House various Sums to supply the Deficiency of their Income, which Sums, together with the Salary allotted to the King's Librarian, yearly amounting to about £. 250, have proved insufficient to defray the necessary Expences of the said Museum, and what now remains in the Hands of the Trustees is not sufficient to carry on the Purposes of the Trust without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to grant such further Support towards enabling them to carry on the Execution of the Trusts reposed in them by Parliament, for the general Benefit of Learning and useful Knowledge, as to the House shall seem meet,

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That there be laid before the House, an Account of Account of the several Sums which have been already Briufh11* granted for the Service of the British Museum, and of Museum, the Expenditure thereof. ordered.

A Petition of the several Persons, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and the other Trustees of the Harbour of , in the County of Cumberland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That several Acts have been passed for preserving, enlarging, and improving, the said Harbour, and Trustees were appointed for carrying the said Acts into Execution; and they were authorized to collect certain Rates and Duties for that Purpose, laid upon Coals and Merchandize imported and exported at, and Shipping using the said Harbour; and that the' Trustees proceeded in the Execution of the Trull re-posed in them, and from Time to Time borrowed several considerable Sums of Money on the Credit of the said Rates and Duties, but the said Harbour being improved, they were enabled to pay off a great Part of the Debt they had contracted as aforesaid, and a large Sum of Money ltill remained in their Hands; and that, in the Year 1798, a voluntary Contribution being set on Foot for the Aid and Assistance of Government, towards carrying on the War against the Enemies of Great Britain, the Trustees thought themselves authorized to pay out of the Money then in their Hands the Sum of £.2,000 to such Subscription, but Doubts have since been suggested, whether they had Authority so to apply that Money; the Petitioners, however, hope that the House will think the Trustees who directed such Application of the Money for so good and laudable a Purpose, should be indemnified for having so done; and that l'ome Doubts have arisen on the Validity of the Elections of the Trustees between the Year Vol. 57.

1710 and the Year 1796, and it is expedient such Doubts should be removed, and the Mode of appointing Trustees in future clearly ascertained; and that the said Acts also require Amendments and Alterations, and Additions: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

11 m!n't Pet, tion of the Hibernian Mine Company, being

Company* offered to be presented to the House,

Petition. - Mr. Bragge (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are Proprietors of a Copper Mine called T Mine, situate at Ballymurtagh, in the Parish of Cry He. Mac Adam, and County of Wick low, in Ireland, and had, previous to the Rebellion of 1798, expended upwards of 60,000 in bringing the Works of the said Mine to Perfection, which were at that Period in a State of pro-grelfive Profit to the Petitioners; and that, at the Time of the breaking out of the Rebellion in May 1798, the Petitioners, having a large Quantity of Gunpowder at their Works, for the Purpose of carrying the same on, by blasting Rocks, and other necessary Works, under Ground, it was thought prudent, by the General Officer commanding His Majesty'sTroops in that Quarter, that the Powder and Iron Tools should be removed; and they were accordingly taken, by a Party of the Antrim Militia, from the Works, and conveyed into the Town of Rath-drum, where they were detained by the Troops for upwards of Eighteen Months; and that, upon the Removal of the Powder and Iron Tools from the Works, the Petitioners were compelled to flop the Working of the Mines, and in consequence thereof, the Water very loon completely flooded them, and the different Houses and Storchouses at Arkloto, contiguous to the said Mines, and belonging thereto, were occupied as Polls and Barracks for His Majesty's Forces; and that, in the' Month of October 1798, the Legislature of Ireland palfed an Act, appointing Commissioners for enquiring into the Losses sustained by His Majesty's loyal Subjects in the said Rebellion, and did thereby limit the Time for making such Claims to a Period of Six Months from the passing of the said Act, videlicet, to the 6th Day of April 1799; and the Commissioners appointed by the said Act did forthwith ilfuc Instructions to Persons intending to claim, whereby they directed, that the Claimant should swear, that he or they had sustained Losses to a certain Amount, and that they should specify the several Articles, and the Value of each respectively, and how such Loss was sustained; and by an Act, passed in the following Session, the Time of putting in Claims was extended from the 1 ft of to the 1 ft of July 1799, on giving a satisfactory Reason for the same not having been put in before; but, by the said last mentioned Act, no Claim could be received, under the second Limitation, to a greater Amount than One Hundred Pounds, lave and except the Claims of certain Persons therein particularly mentioned; and that, from the Nature of the Injury sustained in the Property of the Petitioners, and from the Situation of that Part of the Country where the said Mine lies, it was totally im-

possible for the Petitioners to have put in a Claim pursuant to the Instructions issued by the said Commissioners, for, the Mine having become flooded, it w'as hecessary the same should be cleared of the Water, before it could be ascertained what Injury had been sustained; iand, from the continued disturbed State of the Country; owing to the Hordes of Rebels and Outlaws which infefted the Mountains contiguous to the Works, the Officer commanding the District thought it not prudent , to permit the Company to have their Powder back again, left it should fall into the Hands of the Rebels; by which Means it became impracticable for the Petitioners to proceed to clear the Mines until the latter End of 1799, when the Petitioners proceeded with all the Diligence and Dispatch in their Power, but the same could not be effected until the Month -of March

1800, the Mine being full Eighty Fathom below the:

Surface of the Earth; and that, in the last Session of the Parliament of Ireland, an Act was palfed, whereby it was enacted, that in every same where any Claimant had been prevented from preferring his Claim before the said 1 ft Day of July 1799, by Absence from Ireland, or by any unforeseen or unavoidable Accident, without wilful Neglect in themselves, and that the fame, together with the special Causes of such Omission, should be proved, on Oath, to the Satisfaction of the said Commissioners, the Claim of every such Person Ihculd be received by the said Commissionere, and should be of the same Effect as if tire same had been offered before the said ift Day of July, provided that such Claim be made within Three Months from the passing of the said Act, and that the said Claimant's same should, in every other Respect, be conformable to the Provisions of the said recited Acts; and that, in pursuance of the said Act, the Petitioners did prefer a Claim to the Commissioners for their Losses, in consequence of the Rebellion, the Expence and Charge of restoring and repairing the Mines, and the Loss they sustained, by the same being rendered useless for a Period of Twenty-one Months; and in the said Claim did state, as a Reason for not claiming before, the utter Impossibility of the Petitioners ascertaining their Loss, so as to put in their Claim within the Periods before-mentioned, videlicet, the 6th of April 1799. or the ill Day of July 1799, pursuant to the Acts passed for . that Purpose; and that, on the 5th Day of November

1801, the said Commissioners published a List of Claims admitted for hearing, under the last mentioned Act, in which the Sum of One Hundred Pounds only is allowed to the Petitioners, accompanied with an Observation, that the Claim was for a greater Sum than One 1 iundred Pounds, but the Commissioners did not feel themselves empowered, under the last mentioned Act, to admit it to a greater Amount than One Hundred Pounds; and that the Petitioners conceive the said Commissioners did thereby admit, that the Reason given by the Petitioners for not claiming before was sufficient, and as coming within that Description so clearly pointed out by the said Act, as arising from unforeseen and unavoidable Accident, and not from any wilful Neglect or Default in themselves; and that, if they had felt themselves authorized, they would have granted the Petitioners an adequate Remuneration for their Lolfes: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to authorize the said Commissioners to review and examine the Claim of the Petitioners, and to grant such Recompence for the Petitioners Lolfes as the said Commissioners shall, under the peculiar Circumstances of the Cafe, think just and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioner hath obtained His Majesty's Royal Letters Patent for a new Mode or Process, introduced by him, of Tanning all forts of Hides and Skins, by which Process, Leather, of a Quality equal, if not superior, to the bell hitherto known, is manufactured in about as many Days as it generally requires Months to tan it well in the usual way, and with considerably less Expence of Labour; and that, conceiving, from the Experience of several others, as well as his own, during feme Years, that great Advantages, both Commercial and Financial, might be derived from the general Adoption of this Process, and that it would be a valuable Improvement on so important a Branch of the Trade of the Country as that of Leather, ' the Petitioner submitted his Views on the Subject to the Consideration of the Lords of the Committee of Council for Trade; and that their Lordships, having investigated the Matter with that Attention which its apparent Importance required, were convinced, from the Testimonies, now in their Possession, of several eminent Tanners, Cordwainers, and others, acquainted with the Subject, of the Advantages of the new Process, and of the Necessity of rendering it public, and would have recommended it much sooner to the Lc-giflature had they received the Report of the London Tanners and Curriers

respectUng the Amendments which they might with to be made in the Stat. x fames I, c. 22, which Report their Lord ships had often called for, and long expected; but this Report was obtained only a few Days before the End of the lull Session of Parliament; and that under these Circumstances, and in order to avoid any further Loss of Time, the Petitioner, with the Approbation and Assistance of Gentlemen as distinguished for their Knowledge in Matters of this Nature, as for their Zeal for the Service of the Country', relblved to lay his Patent open to the Public; to this End, printed Directions for Tanning, according to the new Process, have been sent to every Part of the Country, Advertisements have been infcrtecl in the public Papers, inviting and authorizing all the Tanners in the United Kingdom to practise the lame, offering them any further Explanations they might wish for on the Subject, and even the personal Assistance of the Petitioner, if required; this he has performed, as far as Time and other Circumstances would permit; and, as much remains yet to be done, in order totally to remove the Prejudices of Tanners in Favour of their old Habits, the Petitioner is willing to complete this Talk when sufficiently empowered lb to do: And therefore praying the House wiil grant him inch Compensation as they may think his Services entitled to.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others. Proprietors of the T/tames and Medway Canal, and otherwise interested in the Navigation of the River Medway, waspresented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to enable the Wardens and Commonalty of the New Bridge of in the County of

Kent, to complete the Improvements and Repairs of the said Bridge, and to raise Money for that Purpose; and Setting forth. That a Petition hath been presented to the House from the Mayor and Citizens of the City of ter, the great Object of which, from its Allegations and other Information, the Petitioners learn to be, that a Water Toll or Pontage should be imposed upon Vessels passing under the said Bridge; and that the Petitioners, with other Persons, about Two Years since, subscribed a Sum of f. 35,000 and upwards, for the Purpose of making a Canal (to be styled The Thames and Medway Canal) from the River Medway at Rochester to the River Thames at end, and that, under the Sanction of an Act lately passed, they have advanced large Sums of Money in Part of their Subscriptions, and made considerable Progress in their Work; and that a Sum sufficient to accomplish the Alterations and Improvements of the said Bridge, so far as they respect the Navigation, was, previously to their Commencement, advanced to the Wardens of the Bridge by Persons subscribing for the Purpose, and the Wardens not only poflels a very considerable Revenue from Lands and other Sources, applicable to the general Improvements and Alterations of the Bridge, but a Part of the Sum so advanced to them for these Improvements and Alterations, which concern the Navigation, fully adequate to their Completion, yet remains to be applied for that Purpose; and that the proposed Toll or Pontage under the Bridge is perfectly unprecedented, and by its Addition to the Tolls now taken upon the River wa % and those to be received at the Canal, it would so enormoufiy enhance the Charges of Navigation as to occasion an Increase of Land Carriage, and a Continuance of the circuitious Passage round the Nore, and would thereby not merely destroy every Prospect of Advantage to the Proprietors of the Canal, and cause them to be Losers to an incalculable Amount, but prove highly injurious to Commerce and the Public in general: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that they may be heard, by themselves, Agents, or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill, and the proposed Clauses thereof, as may appear detrimental to their Interests, or may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves. Agents, or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Member present informed Your Committee, That several Acts have been passed for preserving, enlarging, and improving, the said Harbour, and Trustees were appointed for carrying the said Acts into Execution, and they were authorized to collect certain Rates and Duties for that Purpose laid upon Coals and Merchandize imported and exported at, and Shipping uling, the said Harbour; that the Trustees proceeded in the Execution of the Trull reposed in them, and, from Time to Time, borrowed several Sums of Money on the Credit of the said Rates and Duties, but the said Harbour being improved, they were enabled to pay off a great Part o^ the Debt they had contracted, and a large Sum of Money still remained in their Hands; that in the Year 1798, a Voluntary Contribution being set on Foot for the Aid and Assistance of Government towards carrying on the War, the Trustees thought themselves authorized to pay out of the Money then in their Hands the Sum of f.2,000 to such Subscription, but Doubts have

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the 33d Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Severn, at Shrewsbury, in the County of Salop, to the River Mersey, at or near Nether pool, in the County of Chester; and also for making and maintaining certain Collateral Cuts from the said Canal, was read: —

And,

Mr. 'Thomas Telford being examined, laid, That by the said Act, certain Persons were united into One Body Corporate, by the Name and Style of " The Company of Proprietors of the Ellesmere Canal f and were authorized

and empowered to make, complete, and maintain, a Canal, navigable and passable for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, from and out of the River Severn, within, the Liberties of the Town of Shrewsbury, in the County of Salop, to unite with the River Mersey, at or near Netherpool, in the County of Chester; and also to make, complete, and maintain, several Collateral Navigable Cuts, to branch from and out of the said Canal, as in the said Act mentioned; and the said Company of Proprietors were by the said Act authorized to raise and contribute amongst themselves, in such Proportion as they should think proper, a competent Sum of Money for making and completing the said Canal, Collateral Cuts, and the Reservoirs, Feeders, Ways, Quays, Wharfs, and other Works and Conveniencies belonging or requisite thereto, not exceeding the Sum of £.400,000, except as therein is mentioned: That if the said Sum should be found insufficient for making and completing the said intended Works by the said Act authorized to be made, and all necessary Charges and Expences relating thereto, the said Company of Proprietors were by the said Act enabled to raise and contribute among themselves, any further or other Sum of Money, for completing the said Undertaking, not exceeding £.50,000; and in case the said Company of Proprietors should be desirous of raising the said Sum of £. 50,000, or any Part thereof, or any further Sum or Sums of Money not exceeding in the Whole £.50,000, in Addition to the said several Sums of £.400,000 and £.50,000, by Mortgage of the said Undertaking, they were, by the said Act, authorized to borrow and take up at Interest all or any Part of the said several Sums of £.50,000 and £.50,000, on the Credit of the said Navigation and Undertaking, in Manner in the said Act mentioned: That the said Company of Proprietors were by the said Act authorized to take and receive, for the Use and Benefit of the said Company, the several Rates therein mentioned for the Tonnage and Wharfage of all Coals, Stone, Timber, Merchandize, and other Goods, Matters, and Things whatsoever, which should be carried or conveyed upon any Part of the said Canal and Collateral Cuts, or any of them; and it was thereby enacted, that none of the said Rates should be payable, demanded, or taken, by virtue of the said Act, for or in respect of any Boat, Barge, or other Vessel, laden with Coal, Coke, Culm, Lime, or Lime Stone only,

which

which might pass or be navigated! dlohg any Part of the said Canal, between Pont Cyfyland the upper End of the Cegedcg Valley, near Byumbo, in the County of Den-

bigh, provided such Boat, Barge, or other Veil'd, should pals or be navigated, with the same Lading, Ten Miles at the lead along any other Part of the said Canal and Collateral Cuts, or any of them, and should pay Tonnage after the Rates in the said Act mentioned for such Ten Miles at the lead, in respect of the same Boat, Barge, or other Veil'd, and the Lading therein: That by several subsequent Acts, passed in the 36th and 41 d Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, the said Company of Proprietors were authorized to vary the Line of the said Canal and Cuts in the said A«d mentioned, and to make, extend, and maintain, several new Branches to communicate therewith: That the Powers given by the said Act. of the 33d of His present Majesty, were, by the said respective Acts of the 36th and 41 d Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, extended, varied, enlarged, and amended; and that the making and maintaining of that Part of the said Canal between Pont Cyfyltee and the upper End of the Ccgedog Valley will be attended with a considerable Expence, and it is reasonable that the said Company of Proprietors should, if they make and maintain the lame, be authorized to have, receive, and take, the like Rates of Tonnage and Wharfage upon and on the Banks thereof, as they are, by the said Act of the 33d Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, authorized to take and receive in respect of Coals, Coke, Calm, Stone, and other 'filings, which shall be carried and conveyed upon any other Part of the said Canal and Collateral Cuts therein mentioned: That Shares, to a considerable Amount, of the said Sum of £.400,000, which was intended to have been originally subscribed by the said Company of Proprietors amongd themselves, for the Purposes of the said Undertaking, were referred for the Land Owners through whole Lands the said Canal and Collateral Cuts were authorized to be made, some of which Land Owners have failed or declined to accept the Shares so reserved for them as aforesaid, or to pay the Calls or Subscriptions thereon, by Reason whereof, and of the Insolvency of some other of the original Subscribers, the Amount of the present Stock of the said Company is reduced to £-333,000, the greatest Part whereof hath been expended in the Prosecution of the said Undertaking, and in carrying the Powers of the said several Acts into Execution; and that the Whole of the said Sum of £.400,000, intended to have been originally raised or contributed by the said Company of Proprietors amongst themselves, for the Purposes of the said Undertaking, will be necessary for the completing the said Canal, Collateral Cuts, and ether W'orks, by the said several recited Acts authorized to be made and executed; and it is expedient thdt the said Company of Proprietors should be authorized and empowered to raise so much Money as shall be necessary to make up the Stock or Subscription of £.400,000, so intended to have been originally raised or contributed, for the Purposes of the said Undertaking as aforesaid, without resorting to the Powers in the said Act of the 33d Year of the Reign of His present Majesty contained, lor railing, by Contribution amongst themselves, of by Mortgage of the said Navigation and Undertaking, the several additional Sums of £. 50,oooo and £.50,000 in the said Act of the 33d Year of His present Majesty mentioned; and that the fakl Company of Proprietors have, in pursuance of the said recited Acts, made and completed a considerable Part of the said Canal and Collateral Cuts; but it is found that the Powers and Provisions of the said recited A els are in Ibmc Respects defective, and it is requisite that the same (houki be altered and amended.

Several Members present informed Your Committee,

That the Improvement of the Line of Communication between Chester, Liverpool, Mane heftier, Leeds, Sheffield, York, and all the North Country manufacturing and commercial Towns of Great Britain as well as of Scotland, and that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, by the Way of Holyhead, through the Counties of Denbigh and Carnarvon, is an Object of great- public Importance, as it would tend to facilitate the Ir.tcrcourse between both Parts of the United Kingdom; — that the Passage over Conzvay River, called Conzvay Ferry, in the County of Carnarvon, is generally attended with very great Delay and Inconvenience, and frequently with Danger, to all Persons travelling over the said Ferry with Mails and Dispatchcs between England and Ireland, and to all other Persons having Occasion to pass and repass that Way. —

And,

the whole Timfc: That, as a Coal Light, it is kept up in as good a State as other Coal Lights, but when the Wind blows from the Well, it is surrounded with Smoke, and the Light very dim; and from a Number of Pit and Limekiln Lights near, frequently not to be distinguished from those; and often one of those has been taken for the Callle Lights, and by miltaking the Castle Lights, Ships have been aground, and considerable Damage has aril'en from the lame, and Ships embayed: That there is an Oil Refiefting Light on the Cromer Lighthouse (Norfolk Coall; on the Principle of that now proposed at Tinmouth, which the Witness has frequently lcen, and

has experienced the Utility of it, and is satisfied it has prevented the Loss of many Vessels. — And the Witness added. An Twer of /TR. Speaker acquainted the House, that the follow-

lord Hutch- JLVJL ing Letter had been received from the Right of Thank*? honourable Lord Hutchinson, in return to the Thanks of this House, signified to him, in Obedience to their Commands of the 18 th Day of

Malta, 28th December 1801.

Sir,

I have received with the utmost Satisfaction and Respect, the unanimous Resolution of the House of Commons, thanking the Generals, the Officers, Non-commissioned Officers, and Privates, of the Army in Egypt, who served under the Command of the late Sir Ralph Abercrombie, for their brilliant, noble, and meritorious Conduct in the Actions of the 8th, 13th, and 21st of March.

I have not failed to communicate your Resolutions to the different Parties concerned, and I am to ashire you, both in their Names and in my own, that nothing can be so grateful to our Feelings as the Approbation of the House of Commons, and the Testimony which they are pleased to bear, that the Army in Egypt has sustained the Honour of their Sovereign, and promoted the Glory of their Country. We know well that we have received One of the greatest Rewards that can be conferred upon British Subjects; and we rest in humble Hope that our future Conduct may not prove us to be entirely unworthy of such Distinction.

I cannot conclude without expressing a Sentiment of

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing, altering, widening, and improving, the Road leading from the City of Canterbury, to the Town and Port of Sandwich, in the County of Kent; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing, altering, widening, and improving, the Road leading from the City of Canterbury to the Town of Rams-gate, in the Isle of Thanet, in the County of Kent; and for suspending and varying, for a limited Time, so much of an Act, passed in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, as relates to the Toll Gate, and to the Tolls now payable by virtue of the said Act, on the Road leading from the said City of Canterbury to the Isle of Thanet; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing the Term, and altering and enlarging the Powers, of Two Acls, passed in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second,' and the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road leading from thcTurnpike Road near the West End of the Town of Chesterfield to Matlock Bridge; and also the Road leading out of the said Road over Darley Bridge to Cross Green; and also the Road leading out of the said last mentioned Road to the Turnpike Road near Rowefley

Bridge, all in the County of Derby -, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Commons and Waste Lands within the Parish of in the North'

Riding of the County of York; without any Amendment: And also*

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for naturalizing Albert Wittenberg; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing the Commons and Wastes within the Manor and Parish of in

the County of Warwick; with an Amendment; to which. Amendment the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also,

other Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being inhabitants of the said Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; ‘viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Samuel Pepys Cockerell being examined, said, That the Tower of the Church belonging to the said Parish, having in the Year 1800 been found to be very ruinous, it became necessary, according to the Report of experienced Architects, that the same should be immediately taken down, which was accordingly done, and a considerable Progress hath been made in Re-building the lame: That by taking down the said Tower, several Parts of the Church were unavoidably damaged, and the said Church is generally very much out of Repair, and the Church-yaid requires, as well by additional Vaults as otherwise, certain Improvements, for the more decent Interment of the Dead, and that these several Improvements will require a considerable Sum to be expended: That the Place used as a Velby Room for the said Parish, was included in the said Tower, very inconveniently situated, in a ruinous State, and much too small: That the Watch House and Engine House were so much out of repair, that it became necessary that they should be taken down, which was accordingly done, and a new Vestry Room, with a Watch House and Engine House, and Vaults under the fame, have been built. — And the Witness further laid. That the Burying Ground adjacent to the said Church, will, in consequence of the increased Population of the Parish, loon become too small, and is incapable of being enlarged; and it is necessary that Provision should be made for the Purchase of a Piece of Ground to be used as a Cemetery, for the said Parish. — Then,

Mr. Emanuel Allen, being examined, said. That the Discharge of the Debts already incurred in the Progress of the Re-building of the said Tower, and the several other Improvements above-mentioned, will, altogether, amount to a large Sum, and that the Money cannot be raised according to the Method prescribed by the Laws now in being, without being very oppressive on the Inhabit.ints of the said Parish, and occasioning considerable Ditlrefs to the poorer Class of Housekeepers. — And being further examined, the Witness said. That the Mode of paying the Stipend to the Rector of the said Parish, by a Special Rate, on the Inhabitants, has been found inconvenient and expensive, and it is conceived it would be more advantageous to the said Inhabitants if a more cafv and lei's expensive Mode of paying the said Stipend were adopted. — And he further said. That the Method of collecting the Rates for the Relief of the Poor of the said Parish hath been found inconvenient, and it would b.e of considerable Advantage if a more speedy and effectual Mode ot collecting the lame, were established: 't hat the Poor of the said Parish are very numerous, and

are supported and maintained in a House provided for their Reception, which House having become too small, it is necessary that Powers should be granted for enlarging the fame, or providing another House in some other Situation; and that it is expedient that Provision should be made for appointing a Clergyman, with an adequate Stipend* to attend and instruct the Poor within the said House, and that proper Regulations should be established for the Management, Employment, and good Government of the Poor, as well within the said House, as all others receiving parochial Relief within the said Parish.

That there are, within the Parish of Spelfbury, certain Commons and Waste Grounds, which, in their present State, are incapable of any considerable Improvement; but, if the same were inclosed, and specific Allotments made to the Persons interested therein, according to their several and respective Rights, great Advantage would be derived to them therefrom. — -And the Witness added, That it will be attended with a great Loss to the Petitioners, if Leave be not given to bring in a Bill for making such Allotments and Inclosure in this present Session.
