A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Hotpreflers, in the City of Norwich, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Glazed Paper 11 fed by the Hotpreflers of that City in dressing Worded Stuffs manufactured there, is, by an Act, made in the 34th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, made liable to an Excise Duty of for every Hundred Weight made in this Country, and of 12J. for every Hundred Weight imported; and that the Petitioners have understood that heavier Duties are about to be imposed on such Paper; and if such Duties should be imposed, the Trade of the City of Norwich will be materially injured: And therefore praying, That no heavier Duty may be imposed on such Glazed Paper than the same is now liable to.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, Manufacturers, and Inhabitants, of the Towns and Neighbourhood of Tipton and Sedgcley in the County of Stafford, whose Names arc thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have long seen, with much Concern, that the Practice of baiting of Bulk is not only disgraceful to Humanity, but is highly prejudicial to the Morals of the lower Order of the People, and materially affects the Industry and Labour of the Persons employed in the Manufactures of the said Towns and Neighbourhood: And therefore praying the House to take the same into Considerationj and to apply such Remedy as shall seem expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Vyner accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House; relative to Paving Bills, and Bills for building Bridges, had been complied with; but it appeared -to the Committee; that the Part of the Petition which relates to supplying the said Town with Water, is not meant to be proceeded upon; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

William Hopkinjon being examined, said, That the Bridge over the River Wit ham, in the Borough of Boston, in the County of Lincoln, is much too narrow', and at present in a very decayed and ruinous State and Condition, and is become inconvenient and dangerous to Passengers,

Carriages, and Cattle, passing the lame; and therefore

it is necessary to ta£e down and re-build the fame, and

also to widen, raise, and render more commodious,

several Streets, Lanes, or Ways, leading or near thereto;

and to purchase and take down several Houses and

Buildings for that Purpose: That the Situation of the

present Bridge is very inconvenient and incommodious,

and therefore it will tend greatly to the Improvement

of the Borough, if the intended Bridge was made and *

erected in a more proper and convenient Situation, very

near the present Bridge; and in such case it will be necessary to purchase and take down several Houses and

Buildings: That the Gaol and House of Correction of

the said Borough is, at present, in a very decayed and

ruinous State, and, by reason of the confined Situation

thereof, and for want of a free Circulation of Air, the fame is become very unhealthy and dangerous to the

Lives of the Persons confined therein; and it is highly

necessary that the said Gaol and House of Correction

should be enlarged, and a proper and suitable Prison

Yard added thereto; and for that Purpose it will be necessary to purchase and take down several Houses and

Buildings: That the Market Crofsof the said Borough,

and several of the Rooms over the fame, which are

appropriated for the TransaClion of public Business

within the said Borough, are too small, and at present

very inconvenient and incommodious; and it is become

necessary that the said Market Crols and Rooms should be enlarged, and made more convenient to Persons re-

sorting thereto, or having Occasion to use the fame. —

And the Witncls added. That it would be highly beneficial to the Town and Neighbourhood of the said Borough, if Powers were, vested in the Petitioners for the better Regulation of the Fairs, Marts, and Markets, held within the said Borough.

Ordered, That the said Report be re-committed.

Ordered, That the said Report be re-committed to the Committee to whom the said Petition was referred.

Petition of A Petition of the Makers or Manufacturers of Milled MiUed*Board, Boajd, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf rcipecting the of themselves and other Makers and Manufacturers of Milled Board, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the disallowinig and taking away the Drawback of the Duty formerly allowed on the Exportation of Milled Board, and the laying an additional Duty thereon during the last Session of Parliament, has greatly injured and prejudiced this Trade so as nearly to prevent the Exportation of Milled Board, and greatly to diminish the Home Consumption thereof, which occasions a Diminution in the Receipt of the Public Revenue, as well by decreeing the Duties a riling from Milled Board as by lessening the Value of the old and useless pitched Cables and Ropes of the Royal Navy, of which the Milled Board is principally made; and that the Petitioners conceive that a Reduction of the Duties on the Home Consumption, and the allowing a Drawback of the Duties, or the greater Part thereof, on the Exportation of Milled Board, would tend to encourage the Trade, and to increase the Revenue: And therefore praying, That the Duties on Milled Boards may be lessened, and that a Drawback may be allowed on all Milled Boards exported, of the whole Duties payable thereon, or of such Part thereof, as to the House shall seem meet; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as the House shall deem expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

That at the Time the Petition for the said Bill was presented to the House, referred to a Committee, and reported upon, (he Petitioner was detained in Ireland by particular Business; and that upon his coming to England, he was induced to cause some Enquiry to be made as to the Proceedings of the Committee, to whom the Petition for Leave to bring in the said Bill was referred; from those Enquiries he has reason to believe, that the Standing Orders of the House, respecting Notices of Applications for Bills of the Nature of that now depending as aforesaid, have not been complied with, inasmuch as the Petitioner can make it appear that The Sligo Journal, in which the Notice of the intended Application for the above Bill was given, is publillied only on a Friday, that such Notice was inserted in The Sligo Journal of Friday the 18 th and 25th Days of September last; that it thereby became impossible, according to the Course of publishing the said Newspaper, to comply with the Standing Order of the House respecting Bills for paving Cities and Towns, bearing Date the 20th Day of May 1791; and that, in order to cure such Defect of want of Notice, an Impression of the said Newspaper, as the Petitioner has heard, was caused to be printed off, bearing Date Tuesday the 29 th of the same Month of September, but whether before or after that Day the Petitioner knows not, but it contained various Articles of News which had been inserted in the Paper of the preceding Friday, but without any Advertisement whatever except that of the Notice for the said Bill; and that the said Newspaper of Tuesday the 29th of September bears the same Number with that of the Newspaper of Friday the 25th of September, and which, the Petitioner apprehends, cannot be Galled a Publication in a Newspaper within the Meaning of the Standing Orders of the House, inasmuch as it was published in Two Numbers only, instead of Three, viz. in Numbers 519 and 520: And therefore praying.

That a Committee may be appointed to enquire how far, and in what Manner, the Standing Orders of the House, in the case of Notices, have been complied with. *

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. FofMr. Bragge, he.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to lend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Ordered, That all who come to the said Committee have Voices.

Ordered, That the Report which, upon the 15th Day Report of March last, was made from the Committee, to whom refem the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and other Inhabitants of the Town of Sligo, in the County of Sligo, was referred, be referred to the said Committee.

A Petition of the Bight honourable Henry Nevill Farl of Abergavenny, and the humble Petition of Thomas

Hill, of Dennis, in the County of Stafford, Esquire, and

Joseph llarrifon, of Nanty Glo, in the County of Mon-

mouth, Gentleman, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making and maintaining certain Railways to communicate with the meuthshire Canal Navigation, and for enabling the Com-

Vol. 57.

pany of Proprietors of that Navigation to raise a further Sum of Money to complete their Undertaking; and for explaining and amending the Acts, passed in the 32d and 37th Years of His present Majesty's Reign, relating thereto; and Setting forth. That the said Earl of Abergavenny is the Owner of a large Tract of Land, abounding with Minerals of Iron and Coal, at and adjoining to Nanty Glo aforesaid, and the said Thomas Hill and Joseph Harrison are the Lessees of the said Premises for a long Term of Years, and they, as well as the former Lessees thereof (whose Interest in the Premises was some Time since purchased by the Petitioner Thomas Hill) have expended very large Sums of Money in erecting Furnaces, Engines, and other Buildings, driving Levels, and making other Works and Conveniencies for working the said Mines, upon the Faith and Assurance that the Provisions and Directions contained in the said Acts, for making a Rail or Waggon Way from near Aberbeeg to Nanty Glo aforesaid, would have beeWduly executed and performed; and the said Lessees were also induced to become Subscribers to the said Undertaking, to a very considerable Amount, for the Purpose of obtaining such Rail or Waggon Way; and that, although the several Sums, authorized to be raised by the said Acts, have been raised by the said Company of Proprietors, no Part of the said Rail or Waggon Way has been made, but the said Sum, specifically set apart and appropriated for that Purpose, ^has been applied, contrary to the expsefs Stipulations and Directions of the said last mentioned Act, to other Uses and Purports; and the said Company of Proprietors now propose to engage in other expensive Works, without completing their original Undertaking, to the great Damage and Injury of the Petitioners; and that the said Bill also contains divers Allegations, Clauses,

Powers, and Provisions, highly injurious to the Rights and Interests of the Petitioners: And therefore praying,

That they may be heard by their Counsel or Agents, against the Allegations, Clauses/ and Provisions, of the said Bill, and that the same may be amended and altered, and that effectual Security may be made by the said Bill, that the Sum before appropriated to the making of the said Rail pr Waggon Way, from near Aberbeeg to Nanty G/o aforesaid, shall be applied out of the first Monies to be raised, by virtue of the said Bill, for that specific Use and Purpose; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices who come to the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Hopkiufon, being examined, said, That the

Bridge over the River Wit ham, in the Borough of , in the County of Lincoln, is much too narrow, and, at present, in a very decayed and ruinous State and Condition, and is become inconvenient and dangerous to Passengers. Carriages, and Cattle passing the fame; and therefore it is necessary to take down and re-build the fame, and also to widen, raile, and render more commodious, several Streets, Lanes, or Ways, leading or near thereto, and to purchase and take down several Houses and Buildings for that Purpose; that the Situation of the present Bridge is very inconvenient and incommodious, and therefore it will tend greatly to the Improvement of the Borough, if the intended Bridge was made and erected in a more proper and convenient Situation, very near the present Bridge; and in such Cale it will be necessary to purchase and take down several Houses and Buildings. — And the Witness further said. That the Gaol and House of Correction of the said Borough, is at present in a very decayed and ruinous State, and, by reason of the confined Situation thereof, and for want of a free Circulation of Air, the same is become very unhealthy, and dangerous to the Lives of the Persons confined therein; and it is highly necessary that the said Gaol and House of Correction should be enlarged, and a proper and suitable Prison Yard added thereto; and for that Purpose it will be necessary to purchase and take down several Houses and Buildings.

Thmfday 6th May.

Mr. William Holmes called in; and examined: — He is in the Army, and generally with his Regiment j his Father lives in the County of Sligo; lived Three Years during the last Six Years with his Father; never knew any Newspaper published at Sligo, by Gray, only upon Fridays; his Father subscribed to the Paper; he was in the Habit of calling for this Paper for his Father, and never called oftener than Once a Week.

Was you at your Father's at Sligo, the 29th September 1801 ?---1 went to my Father's House before the

First of September, and left it on the 2d of October', I was, during the whole of that Time, in the County, visiting about: I rather think I was at my Father's on that Day.

Did you ever hear of any other Paper published, than those produced to the Committee, dated on Fridays ? ----- Not for the last Five Years. Withdrew'.

A Member present informed the Committee, That he has know'n the County of Sligo for Twelve or Thirteen Years, and has been there for Six or Seven Weeks together every Year, and never knew of any other Sligo Journal but a Friday Paper published by Gray, and which he ahways considered as a Weekly Paper; he was there last Chr if mas, and there was only One Weekly Paper published, w'hich w'as dated on a Friday.

The Earl of Kingston, called in; and examined: — Has known Sligo a long Time, but never knew any but a Weekly Paper published there; has not been at for Three Years; nearer Four. Withdrew.

Is it a public Coffee Room ?--- It is.

not, otherwise than having them sent to the Stamp Office.

Would the Paper of the 29th have been

published, but at your special Desire ?----1 believe it

Time of November.

What is the general Time a Mail is going from London to Sligo ?--Six Days.

----1 can't lay; but think he ought to have done it; I

should think he did. Withdrew.

A Petition of Edward Fowle, of the Parish of Boxley, petition of in the County of Kent, Gentleman, on Behalf of himself, and several of the Inhabitants of the adjoining Parishes, Mefwsy Na-was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of vigatioa Bill, the Bill for repealing an Act, passed in the 32d Year of His present Majesty's Reign, for improving the Navigation of the River Medway, from the Town of Maidstone, through the several Parishes of Maidstone, Boxley, Ailing-ton, and Aylesford, in the County of Kent, and for the better and more effectually improving the Navigation of the said River; and Setting forth, That all the public, useful, and beneficial Purposes of the said Bill, could be obtained without that Infringement of the Rights of the Petitioner, and the other Inhabitants of the said Parishes, which the Bill will create and perpetuate; and that, in passing a Clause in the said Act of the 32d Year of His present Majesty, the House was deceived by the Milre-presentations of those whose Interest it was to earn' the said Act through the House, by Hating that to be pri- * vate Property which had, from Time immemorial, been devoted to the Public, and by depriving the Petitioner, - and the other Inhabitants of the Parish of Boxley, of an open, ancient, and Kingsway, without providing any Substitute for their Convenience, or Compenfetion for the Injuries they sustain; and that Castle Shelf, mentioned in the said Act as a Ford or Ferry, belonging to Lord Romney, never was a Ferry, nor could in the Nature of Things be used as such; that it was a Shallow running across the River Medway, covered at Low Water not more than Twelve Inches in Depth, and was always con- _ lidered as a public and open Kingsway for all Persons to , pals and re-pass at their rleafure; apd that, at the Time

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Member present informed the Committee, That the Petitioners have long fullered the greatest Inconvenience from the Want of proper Harbours in the Bay of Thurso, whether at the Entrances into the River of Thurso, or at the Road of Scrabjier, situated therein; that it would tend greatly to the Safety and Protection of Vessels navigating the North Sea to have such Harbours formed, and the fame* would also elsentially contribute to the Improvement of the Fisheries on the Northern Coasts of the Kingdom, as well as promote, encourage, and extend the growing Trade and Manufactures of the said Town and adjacent Country; that the Petitioners have subscribed certain Sums of Money for making the said Harbours; and they, with the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Town and Neighbourhood, are willing to be subjected to the Payment of certain Rates, Assessments, and Duties, for maintaining the said Harbours.

Mr. Henry Alexander, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to considerof an Act, made in the 25th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for granting a Stamp Duty on Licences to be taken out by Persons uttering or vending Medicines, and certain Stamp Duties on Medicines fold under such Licences, or under the Authority of His Majesty's Letters Patent, the Resolutions which the Committee had dire cted him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties payable upon every Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Inciolure, containing any Drugs, Oils, Waters, Eflcnces, Tinctures, Powders, and other Preparation or Composition whatsoever, uled or applied, or to be used or applied, externally or internally, as Medicines or Medicaments for the Prevention or Cure, or Belief, of any Disorder or Complaint incident to, or in any.viie adeeming, the Human Body, which shall be uttered or vended in Great Britain, shall ccafe and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for ami upon every Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Inciolure, containing any Drugs, Oils, Waters, Li fences, Tinctures, Powders, or other Preparation or Composition whatsoever, uled or applied, or to be used or applied, externally or internally, as Medicines or Medicaments for the Prevention, Cure, or Relief, of any Disorder or Complaint incident to, or in anywise affecting, the Human Body, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty, according to the Rates following; that is to say: Where any such Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Inciolure aforesaid, with its Contents, shall not exceed the Price or Value of One Shilling, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of One Penny Halfpenny; and where any such Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Inciolure afore-ihid, with its Contents, shall exceed the Price or Value of One Shilling, and not exceed the Price or Value of Two Shillings and Sixpence, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Three Pence; and where any such Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Inciolure aforesaid, with its Contents, shall be above the Price or Value of Two Shillings and Sixpence, and under the Price or Value of Four Shillings, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Sixpence; and where any such Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Inclosure aforesaid, with its Contents, shall be above the Price or Value of Four Shillings, and under the Price or Value of Ten Shillings, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of One Shilling; and where any such Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Inclosure aforesaid, with its Contents, shall be above the Price or Value of Ten Shillings, and under the Price or Value of Twenty

Shillings, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Two Shillings; :and where, any such Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Inclosure aforesaid, with its Contents, shall be above the Price or Value of Twenty Shillings, and under the Price or Value of One Pound Ten Shillings, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Three Shillings; and where any such Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Iticlosure aforesaid, with its Contents, shall be above the Price or Value of One Pound Teh Shillings, and under the Price or Value of Two Pounds Ten Shillings, there shall be charged -a Stamp Duty of Ten Shillings; and where any such Packet, Box, Bottle, Phial, or other Inclosure aforesaid, with its Contents, shall be of the Price or Value of Fifty Shillings, or upwards, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Twenty Sinkings. . ... t

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person in Great Britain uttering or vending any Drugs, Oils, Waters, Essences, Tinctures, Powders, or other Preparations or Gompositions whatsoever, used or applied, or to be used. or applied, externally or internally, as Medicines or Medicaments for the Prevention, Cure, or Relief, of any Disorder or Complaint incident to, or in anywise affecting, the Human Body, shall annually take out a Licence for that Purpose. '

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for and upon every Licence so taken out by any such Person, who shall reside within the Cities of London or Westminster, the Borough of Southwark or within the Limits of the Twopenny Post, or within the City of Edinburgh, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Forty Shillings; and for and upon every Licence, so taken out by any other such Perlen, there shall be charged a Stamp Duty of Ten Shillings.

A Petition of the Court of Directors of the Sierra Leone Company, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, having been incorporated by Act of Parliament, have endeavoured to establish a British Colony at Sierra Leone, with a View of

contributing to the Civilization of Africa, and promoting a more extended Trade in African Produce; and that a considerable Number of Black Colonists from Nova Scotia, and also of Maroons from Jamaica, have been admitted into the said Settlement, by the Reception of whom the British Government has been released

from

Committee of Way* and Means.

Petition of the Sierra Leone Company, fer Leave to present a Petition for Afliltanee.

from Expence, and the Company subjected to great Burthens; and that the Petitioners, through the War as well as other Causes, have met with heavy Losses, and have been for tome Time unable to maintain their African HlbibJishment without Aid from Parliament; and that the real'onable Hopes of Success which the Petitioners had entertained have been hitherto frustrated, chiefly by the War, and other temporary Causes; and that the Petitioners have lately received Advice of an Attack on the Colony having been made by the Natives of Africa, in conllquence of which the Completion of the Fort, and the Maintenance of some Military Force, appear to have become absolutely necessary to the Security of the Settlement, and to the due Protection of the Colonilts; and that the Petitioners submit to the Judgment of the House, that the Objects which they have had in View will be much more effectually promoted, if Parliament Avail think proper to enlarge the Sum which they have been pleased Annually to grant towards the Maintenance of the Civil Establishment of the Company; and that the Petitioners conceive that, besides the Considerations already spoken of, very important National Objects may be promoted by the firm Establishment of a British Colony at Sierra Leone; and that the above-mentioned Advices from Sierra Leone were not received until after the Time limited for receiving Petitions for Private Bills was expired: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to exhibit a Petition, for the Purpose above mentioned.

the several Purishes of Alaidstone, Boxley, Aliington, and Aylesford, in the County of and for the better and more effectually improving the Navigation of the said River; and Setting forth, That the Advantages, if any, arising from the Works proposed by the Bill, can be participated only by Persons who do or may navigate the said River with Vessels and Barges of larger Burthen than those uled by the Petitioners, the Locks on that Part of the Navigation of the said River, of which they are Proprietors (and which Locks are Fourteen in Number) not allowing for a Vessel of more than Forty Tons

Burthen to pass the fame, and all the Vessels employed by the Petitioners are built of that Size; and that the Petitioners will be materially injured should they be compelled to pay any further Tolls or Duties for navigating the said River, within the Distriift mentioned in the said Act of the 3 2d Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, than those which they are liable to pay by the Provisions of the same Act: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect their Rights and Interests; and that Provision may be made therein for exempting the Petitioners from the Payment of any additional Rates or Duties that may be laid by such intended Act; or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises, as. to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Henry Alexander, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it

was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same rwere read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of One Million Five Hundred Thousand Pounds Sterling, being One Million Six Hundred and Twenty-five Thousand Pounds Irish Currency, be raised by Annuities or Debentures, for the Service of Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Contributor to the said Sum shall, for every Ninety-one Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Eleven Pence contributed and paid, be entitled to the Principal Sum of One Hundred Pounds in Annuities, after the Rate of £.3. 1 or. per Centum per Annum, to commence from the 25th Day of December 1801, or, at his Option, be entitled to have and receive a Debenture from the Treasury of Ireland, for the Principal Sum of/. 100, bearing an Interest of £-3- 10 s.per Centum per to commence from the said 25th Day of December 1S01:

That the said Annuities, after the Rate of 3. 10s. per Centum per Annum, shall be added to, and made One-Joint Stock with, the present f. 3. 10 per Centum Annuities, and be payable and transferable at the Bank of Ireland, at the same Time, and in the same Manner, as the said Annuities:

That the said Annuities, or the Interest on the said Debentures, shall be charged and chargeable upon, and payable out of, the Consolidated Fund of Ireland:

That every Contributor shall, on or before the 15th Day of this Instant May, make a Deposit of £. 10 per Centum on such Sum as he or she shall chuse to subscribe, either with the Chief Cashier or Cashiers of the Governor and Company of the Bank of Ireland, or with the Teller and Cashier of His Majesty's Exchequer at Dublin, as a Security for making the future Payments on or before the Days or Times herein after mentioned; that is to lay:

£. 10 per Centum on or before the 18th Day of June 1802;

£. 10 per Centum on or before the 20th Day of then next following;

£. 15 per Centum on or before the 20th Day of then next following;

/. 15 per Centum on or before the 27 th Day of September then next following £. 10 per Centum on or before the 23d Day of Oilolcr then next following;

£. 1; per Centum on or before the 27th Day of November then next following; And,

£. 1 5 per Centum on or before the 30th Day of December then next following:

That every Contributor who Hull make any of the Payments aforesaid before the Times they are respectively payable, shall be allowed an Interest, by way of Discount, after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum on the Sum lb advanced, to be computed from the Day of paying in the same to the Time the same is payable as aforesaid:

That all the Monies to be received by the said Cashier or Cashiers of the Governor and Company of the Bank of Ireland, shall be paid into the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer at Dublin, and, together with any other Monies-received for Debentures as herein before-mentioned, shall be carried to, and form Part of, the Consolidated Fund of Ireland.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed. That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to ashire His Majesty, that we have taken into our most serious Consideration the Definitive Treaty of Peace which His Majesty has been graciously pleated to communicate to this House:

That we acknowledge, with all Humility and Sub-mirtion, His Majesty's undoubted Prerogative of Peace and War: And that we shall consider it to be our first Duty, as far as may depend on us, to maintain inviolate the Public Faith, as it is pledged by this Treaty, and to assist His Majesty in performing, with Uprightness and Punftuality, the Engagements into which His Majesty has been advised to enter:

But that we cannot conceal the painful Apprehensions with which we consider the Relult of those Engagements; nor can we forbear to offer to His Majesty our humble and dutiful Advice for the Adoption of such Measures as can alone, in our Opinion, under the Blessing of Providence, avert from us the Dangers with which we are now surrounded:

That it is impossible for us to have seen, without the utmost Anxiety and Alarm, all the unexampled Circumstances which have attended the final Conclusion of the present Peace: — The extensive and important Sacrifices, which, without any corresponding Concession, this Treaty has added to those already made on our Part by the Preliminary Articles: — The unlooked-for and immense Accessions of Territory, Influence, and Power, which it has tacitly confirmed to — The nume-

rous Subjects of clalhing Interest and unavoidable Dit-pute which it has left entirely unadjusted: And, above

all, those continued and systematic Projects of Aggran-disement, of which, in the very Moment of Peace, we have fecn, unhappily, such undeniable and convincing Evidence:

That, by relinquishing so many Sources of Prosperity in Peace, and so many Bulwarks of Defence in War, and, by renouncing, at the same Time, the Advantage and Security always hitherto derived from the accustomed Renewal of former Treaties, the Government has

imposed on itself a greater Necessity than has ever before existed for Measures of.increased Precaution, and for Determinations of unlhaken Constancy:

That we, therefore, rely on His Majesty's paternal Wisdom for a watchful and unremitted Attention to the Situation and future Conduct of the Power with whom we have negociated; and we think it necessary more especially to allure His Majesty of our ready and firm Support in that Determination which, we trust, His Majesty will henceforward Readily pursue, of refilling every fresh Encroachment (of whatever Nature) which shall be attempted on the Maritime, Commercial, or Colonial Rights and Interefis of the Empire:

This our solemn Declaration, mull, as we believe, materially conduce to prevent the Necessity which it is calculated to meet; and we trust that His Majesty will ailo approve of our Desire to support it by a Scale of Naval and Military Defence, adequate to the Extent of our Danger, and to the Importance of the Interests which we have to maintain:

The Anxiety which we feel in this respect, is the necessary Consequence of our sincere Wilh for the Permanence of the Public Tranquillity which His Majesty has now re-established: And it is for the same important Purpol'e, that we also moll earnestly recommend to His Majesty s Wisdom the prclfing Necessity of arranging, by immediate and amicable Discussion, those Points of essential interest which had been adjusted by former Treaties, but for which no Provision has been made in this Negociation:

These Councils we submit to His Majesty with Confidence, in the present awful Crisis of Public Affairs, prepared to meet with Firmness all the Difficulties and Dangers of our present Situation, but desirous, above all Things, to promote the Stability and Security of real Peace , the Obje<fl which it has been His Majesty's benevolent Desire, by such extensive Sacrifices, to enlure to His loyal and affectionate People.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out from the first Word " That," in the Second Paragraph, to the End of the Question, in order to inlert these Words: " We have already dedared our full Approbation of the Preliminary Articles of Peace, which, by His Majesty's Command, " were laid before this House; and we are satisfied that " His Majesty has, on the Whole, wifely consulted the " Interests of His People in having concluded a Definitive Treaty, founded on the Basis of these Prelimiturics: That, although we deeply lament the " calamitous Events which have taken place on the " Continent of Europe in the Course of the W'ar, we " cannot but refledf, with the ut moll Satisfaction, that " the wild and dcllructive Designs W'ith which this " C'ountry was threatened at its Commencement, have " been effectually frullrated: That His Majesty's Dominions have not only been preservd entire, but u valuable and important Acquisitions have been an- nexed to them: 'Hurt our Commercial and Maritime " Superiority have been maintained and improved; and " that we continue in the confirmed Post'eflion of those " Means of Exertion which the Experience of the late " Contest has proved more than ever to be equal, even " amidst the new and unexampled Difficulties of other " Nations of Europe, to maintain the Independence, " and assert the Honour of this Country: That, im- prefle l with these Sentiments, wc are, on our Parts, u tarncllly iblicitous to cultivate and improve the 3

" Blessings of Peace, and to concur in such Measures " as His Majesty, in His Wisdom, shall judge to be " bell calculated to prevent Occasions of MisunderHanding with Foreign Powers: That we rely on His Majesty's known Disposition to adhere, with the most " scrupulous Fidelity, to His Engagements; but that " we entertain, at the same Time, a perfect Confidence, " that His Majesty will not fail to employ that Vigilance " and Attention which the present Situation of Europe " demands; and, above all, that His Majesty will be " uniformly determined, and prepared to defend, against " every Encroachment, the great Sources of the Wealth, " Commerce, and Naval Power of the Empire: That " we are fully persuaded that His Majesty's faithful " Subjects will, at all Times, be ready to support the " Honour of His Majesty's Crown, and the Rights, " Laws, and Liberties of their Country, with the same " Zeal, Energy, and Fortitude, which they have invariably manifelled during the War now happily " brought to a Conclusion."

And the Question being proposed, That the Words proposed to be left out. Hand Part of the Question;

And a Debate arising in the House thereupon;

And the House having continued to fit till near Three of the Clock on Friday Morning;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the Debate be adjourned till Four of the Clock this Afternoon;

The House divided.

The 1 louse resumed the adjourned Debate on the Amendment which was, Yesterday, proposed to be made to the Motion, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to allure His Majesty that we have taken into our most lerious Consideration the Definitive Treaty of Peace which His Majesty has been graciously plealed to communicate to this House:

That we acknowledge, with all Humility and Submission, His Majesty's undoubted Prerogative of Peace and War; and that we shall consider it to be our first Duty, as far as may depend on us, to maintain inviolate the Public Faith, as it is pledged by this Treaty, and to affilt His Majesty in performing, with Uprightness and Punftuality, the Engagements into which His Majesty has been advised to enter:

But that we cannot conceal the painful Apprehen-fions with which we consider the Relult of those Engagements; nor can we forbear to offer to His Majesty our humble and dutiful Advice for the Adoption of such Measurcs as can alone, in our Opinion, under the Blelfing of Providence, avert from us the Dangers with which we are now Unrounded:

That it is impossible for us to have seen, without the utmost Anxiety and Alarm, all the unexampled Circumstances which have attended the final Conclusion of the present Peace: — The exienfiveand important Sacrifices, which, without any corresponding Concession, this Treaty has added to those already made on our Part by the Preliminary Articles: — The unlooked-for and im-menle Accessions of Territory, Influence, and Power, which it has tacitly confirmed to France: — The numerous Subjects of clalhing Interest and unavoidable Dispute which it has left entirely unadjusted; and above all, those continued and systematic Projects of Aggrandilcment, of which, in the very Moment of Peace, w'e have seen, unhappily, such undeniable and convincing Evidence:

That, by rciinquishing so many Sources of Prosperity in Peace, and so many Bulwarks of Defence in War, and by renouncing, at the same Time, the Advantage and Security always hitherto derived from the accustomed Renewal of former Treaties, the British Government has imposed on itself a greater Necessity than has ever before existed for Mcalures of increased Precaution, and for Determinations of unlhuken Constancy:

Vo L.57.

That we, therefore, rely on His Majesty's paternal Wisdom, for a watchful and unremitted Attention to the Situation and future Conduct of the Power with whom we have negociated; and w'e think it necessary more especially to allure His Majesty of our ready and firm Support in that Determination, which, we trull, His Majesty will henceforward steadily pursue, of refilling every fresh Encroachment (of whatever Nature) which shall be attempted on the Maritime, Commercial, of Colonial Rights and Interests of the British Empire:

This our solemn Declaration must, as we believe, mar terially conduce to prevent the Necessity which it is calculated to meet; and we trull that His Majesty will also approve of our Desire to support it by a Scale of Naval and Military Defence, adequate to the Extent of our Danger, and to the Importance of the Interests which we have to maintain:

The Anxiety which we feel in this Respect, is the necessary Consequence of our sincere Wilh for the Permanence of the Public Tranquillity which His Majesty has now re-established; and it is for the same important Purpose, that we also moll earnestly recommend to His Majesty's Wisdom the pressing Necessity of arranging, by immediate and amicable Discussion, those Points of essential Interest which had been adjusted by former Treaties, but for which no Provision has been made in this Negociation:

These Councils we submit to His Majesty with Confidence, in the present awful Crisis ol Public Aftairs, prepared to meet, with Firmness, all the Difficulties and Dangers of our present Situation, but desirous, above all Things, to promote the Stability and Security of real Peace; the Object which it has been His Majesty's benevolent Desire, by such extensive Sacrifices, to insure to His loyal and affectionate People.

And the Amendment being again proposed, to leave out from the first Word " That " in the Second Paragraph, to the End of the Question, in order to insert, "We have already declared our full Approbation of " the Preliminary Articles of Peace, which, by His Majesty's Command, were laid before this House; and " we are satisfied that His Majesty has, on the whole, " wifely conliilted the Interests of His People, in having " concluded a Definitive Treaty, founded on the Balls " of these Preliminaries: — That, although we deeply " lament the calamitous Events which have taken place " on the Continent of Europe in the Course of the War, " we cannot but refled, with the utmost Satisfaction, " that tire wild and destrudive Deligns with which this " Country was threatened at its Commencement, have " been effectually frustrated: — That His Majesty's Dominions have not only been preserved entire, but valuable and important Acquisitions have been annexed " to them: — That our Commercial and Maritime Superiority have been maintained and improved; and " that we continue in the confirmed Possession of those " Means of Exertion, which the Experience of the late " Con tell has proved more than ever to be equal, even " amidst the new and unexampled Difficulties of other " Nations of Europe, to maintain the Independence, and " assert the Honour of this Country: — That, impressed " with these Sentiments, we are on our Parts earnestly " solicitous to cultivate and improve the Blessings of " Peace, and to concur in such Measures as His Majesty, in His Wisdom, shall judge to be bell calculated " to prevent Occasions of Misunderstanding with Foreign Powers: — That we rely on His Majesty's known " Disposition to adhere, with the moll scrupulous Fide- lity, to His Engagements; and that, in order to indemnify the said Corporation as to such Expences, it is necessary that the Monies lo becoming due to them should be recoverable in a summary Way; and that, by the said Act, Power is given to the Petitioners to make Bye Laws for the regulating of the said Graving Docks, and to lay Penalties on the Breach of the same Bye Laws, not exceeding Forty Shillings for each Offence; and that it is found, by Experience, that the said Penalty is by no Means adequate to the Prevention of the Injuries frequently done through the Carelessness or Milconduft of various Persons, not only to the said Docks, but also to the Machines and other Appendages of such Docks, and it is expedient that the Amount of the said Penalties should be increased; Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Amount of the Annual Sums applicable, under the Acts of the Twenty-sixth and Thirty-second Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, to the Reduction of the National Debt, as the said Sums flood on the ift Day of February 1802, if consolidated into one Sinking Fund, with the additional Sum of Two Hundred Thousand Pounds per Annum, and continually applied at Compound Interest, but without the Addition of any Sums arising from Annuities which may expire, or from Savings of Interest on Annuities which may be reduced, would redeem the Whole of the existing Capital of the National Debt, including the Capital to arise from the Loan of the present Year, within Forty-five Years from the presentTime, and in a shorter Period than the Whole of the said Capital would be redeemed by the separate Application of the said Annual Sums respectively, together with the additional Sum of Two Hundred Thousand Pounds per Annum, as well as of One per Cent, on the Capital to be provided for in the present Year, and of any other Sums which would, by virtue of the said A As, become applicable to the Discharge of such Capital.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,-That the additional Sum of Two Hundred Thousand Pounds per Annum be granted to His Majesty, from and after the 5th Day of January 1803, to be vested in the Commissioners appointed under the said Act of the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient to provide that the Amount of the Annual Sums applicable under the Acts of the Twenty-sixth and Thirty-second Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, to the Reduction of the National Debt, as the said Sums flood on the ift Day of February 1802, should be consolidated into One Sinking Fund, with the additional Sum of Two Hundred Thousand Pounds per Annum, and be continually applied at Compound Interest to the Redemption of the Whole of the existing Capital of the National Debt, including the Capital to arise from the Loan of the present Year.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Sum which may arise from Annuities which tnay expire, or from Savings of Interest on Annuities which may be reduced, shall be applicable to the Public Service, in such Manner as Parliament shall direct.

The laid llcfo'utions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Answrr to Lord Viscount Stopford reported to the House, That Addreu. their Address of Friday last (to allure His Majesty, that we have taken into our most serious Consideration the Definitive Treaty of Peace, which His Majesty has been graciously pleased to communicate to this House: — That we have already declared our full Approbation of the Preliminary Articles of Peace, which, by His Majesty's Command, were laid before this House; and we are satisfied that His Majesty has, on the Whole, wifely consulted the Interests of His People in having concluded a Definitive Treaty, founded on the Basis of these Preliminaries: — That, although we deeply lament the calamitous Events which have taken place on the Continent of Europe in the Course of the War, we cannot but reflect, with the utmost Satisfaction, that the wild and destructive Designs with which this Country was threatened at its Commencement,'have beep effectually frustrated: — That His Majesty's Dominions have not only been preserved entire, but valuable and important Acquisitions have been annexed to them: — That our Commercial and Maritime Superiority have been maintained and improved; and that we continue in the confirmed Possession of those Means of Exertion which the Experience of the late Contest has proved more than ever to be equal, even amidst the new and unexampled Difficulties of other Nations of Europe, to maintain the Independence, and assert the Honour of this Country: — That, impressed with these Sentiments, we are on our Parts earnestly solicitous to cultivate and improve the Blessings of Peace, and to concur in such Measures as His Majesty, in His Wisdom, shall judge to be best calculated to prevent Occasions of Misunderstanding with Foreign Powers: — That we rely on His Majesty's known Dii to adhere with the most scrupulous Fidelity to His Engagements; but that we entertain, at the same Time, a perfect Confidence, that His Majesty will not fail to employ that Vigilance and Attention which the present Situation of Europe demands; and above all, that H is Majesty will be uniformly determined, and prepared, to defend against every Encroachment the great Sources of the Wealth, Commerce, and Naval Power, of the Empire: — That we arc fully persuaded that His Majesty's faithful Subjects will at all Times be ready to support the Honour of His Majesty's Crowm, and the Rights Laws, and Liberties, of their Country, with the same Zeal, Energy, and Fortitude, which they have invariably manifested during the War, now happily brought to a Conclusion) had been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty was plealed to receive the same very graciously.

Mr. Henry Alexander, according to Order, reported Report on from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it so^Inting was referred to consider of Two Acts, made in the 19th Exdie Duties; and 28th Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, relating to the Duties on Auctioneers and Auctions, and for amending several Laws relative to the Excise; and who were inltructed to consider of so much of an Act, made in the 27th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, as relates to the Allowances for Soap and Starch made use of in the Woollen, Linen, and Cotton Manufactories, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Cleric's

Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient to exempt Estates, Goods, and Effects, bought in for the Owner by his Steward or Agent, or under a Notice signed by the Owner's Steward or Agent and the intended Bidder, from the Duty payable on Sales by Auction.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient to exempt Goods and Merchandize imported from any British Colony or Settlement in America, or from the United States of America, from the Duty payable on Sales by Auction on the first Sale thereof, on Account of the Importer, within Twelve Months after the Importation of such Goods and Merchandize.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the several Allowances granted by an Act, made in the 27th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, on Soap and Starch made use of in the Woollen, Linen, and Cotton Manufactories, do cease and determine.

The laid Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the Sugar Coopers of the City of London, whole Names are thereunder-written, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the Petitioners have been obliged to serve Apprenticeships to their said Trade, and to be free of the City of London, and many of them, having no other Occupations, are wholly dependent thereon for Support of themselves and Families; and, if the said Bill should pass into a Law as it now Hands, the Trade of the Petitioners will be diverted into another Channel; and they conceive that Compensation should be made for the Injury which mull accrue to them, in the same Manner as has been granted to other Persons whose Interests are and may be affected by the said Act of the 39th Year of His Majesty's Reign: And therefore praying to be heard, upon the -Report of the said Bill, by themselves, and their Counsel; and that the House will grant to the Petitioners such Relief in the Premises as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is re-committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves and Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all who come to the said Committee have Voices.

ctiiion for Mr. Mainwaring reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, St. Margaret's and others, the Vestry of the Parish of Saint Margaret, Wuirted ^infer, was referred; That the Committee had

,e*K>rtu ' examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had di-

rected him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, it appeared to the Committee, That the Petitioners, in the Month of February 1799, presented a Petition to the House, Bating, amongst other Things, that the Parish Church of Saint Margaret was a very ancient one, and for a Century pall had been, and then was, considered as the Church peculiarly applicable to the religious Purposes of the House; and that the said Parish Church was then in a very defective State, particularly in its external Walls; and the Petitioners had caused the same to be surveyed by an eminent Architect and Surveyor, and, in his Judgment, the Sum of £.6,721. 18s. 4d. was necessary to effect the necessary Repairs thereof; and that thereupon the House was pleased to grant the said Sum of £.6,721. 18s. 4d. which the Petitioners have duly received. — Then,

Samuel Pepys Cockerell, Esquire, Surveyor, being examined, said, That immediately after the Grant was made, the Petitioners proceeded in the several necessary Works, and previously entered into various special Contracts with the several Tradesmen for the Performance thereof; and that the Ellimates, made with a View to the said former Occasions, were formed on the absolutely necessary Repairs, without any Allowances therein for Superintendance of the Works, Fees of Office, Contrails with Workmen, and various other contingent Expences; and in the Progress of the said Repairs, it was discovered, that the Plates and other Timbers under the Roof of the said Church ;were so much decayed, that an entire new Ceiling was thought necessary, and various Alterations and Improvements were also necessary, with a View to the better Accommodation of the Speaker, and other Members of the 1 louse; and attending also to the Unity of Character throughout the Building, new Arrangements, and some Alterations were made, variant to the original Designs, which (together with the Circumstances before-mentioned) have contributed greatly to an In-crealc of the former Ellimates; and that the said Repairs have been nearly accomplished; but the Whole of the said Grant or Sum of £.6,721 (less only by the Sum of £.539. 18s. 6 d. now in the Hands of the Treasurer of the said Parish) has been already exhausted by Payments to the several Tradesmen on Account of their several Works, and in Payment also of the usual Fees of Office, with other considerable yet necessary Expences: That the Monies now remaining due to the said several Contractors, and others, for Work already done, and the Account of Works absolutely necessary to be done finally to cfleCl the said Repairs, will amount to the Sum of £.4,349. 9s. $d. first allowing for the said Sum VOL.57.

of £. 539. i8j\ 6 d.in the Hands of the said Treasurer; and without any jegard being had to the necessary Expences attendant upon this Application.' — Then,

Cotton and other elastic Goods, hath discovered and invented a new and improved Method of retaining (Cotton in particular) beyond any hitherto invented or now in Use, the Performance of which being not only as cafy and expeditious as the ordinary Mode, but lets expensive, by effecting a considerable Saving both in Package and Freight, will be advantageous to the Commercial and Manufacturing Interests of this Country, and of great public Utility; and that the Petitioner lately applied to the East India Company, requelling their Encouragement for carrying his Design into Effect, by granting him a Per-Centage on all Cotton that shall be imported into this Country or China, or into any of the Ports of India, on the Company's own Account, which shall be retained after the Process invented by him, to which they have acceded, on the express Condition that the Company, as well as Individuals, be left at full Liberty cither to make Use of the Petitioner's Method of retaining, or not, as they shall judge proper; and that the Petitioner conceives, when his newly-invented Mode of retaining Cotton shall be disclosed to the Public, it will be deemed so highly beneficial as to be speedily and generally adopted in Practice, and will prove of (lill greater Bencht to the India and Foreign Importers, from the more considerable Improvement and Saving it will be to them in Package and Freight, than to those of the East Indies, the present ordinary Mode of Packing in Use with both the former being so much looser than, and inferior to, that of the East India Traders, whence the India and Foreign Merchants will derive so much more considerable Advantage to themselves, in the Article of Package and Freight, as to enable and induce them cheerfully to pay, 0

out of their thereby increased Profits, the same Premium which he has been willing lo accept from the East India Company, and the Individuals enjoying a permissive Trade under them; and that the Petitioner therefore humbly proposes, on having a proportionable Allowance secured to him on the Gross Sale Value , of all Cotton imported from the West Indies, and Foreign Parts,'retained after the Process invented by him, and also on having his aforesaid Agreement with the India Company established, and rendered effectual by the Authority of the Legislature, to make a full Disclosure and clear Specification of his newly-invented Method of retaining Cotton, so as to enable the Public to enjoy the Benefit of that Improvement; and that the Petitioner, being engaged in perfecting the said Invention, and in submitting the Arrangement he had made with the East India Company to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, with the View of engaging their Attention to the Matters Hated in his said Petition, was not till lately apprized that the Time for presenting Private Petitions was expired: And therefore praying,

MR. Speaker acquainted the House, That the follow* ing Letter had been received from the Right honourable Lord lint chin [on, in Return to the Thanks of this House, signified to him in Obedience to their Commands of the i 2th Day of November last.

Turin, 8th May 1802.

Sir,

1 had left Malta before the Thanks of the House of Commons to the Army serving in Egypt had been received, they therefore did not reach me till many Months after they had been voted. I shall ever retain a proud and grateful Sense of the Honour which the House of Commons has been pleased to confer upon me. The able Assistance of the General Officers acting under my Command, the Order, Valour, and Discipline of the Troops, made my Duty a Talk of easy Performance, and at length led to that final and fortunate liiue which has lo juilly obtained them the Approbation of their Sovereign, and the Applause of their Country.

I have the Honour to be,

Sir,

With great Regard,

Your obedient humble Servant,

Hutchinson.

The Right honourable The Speaker of the House of Commons, &c.&c. &c.

Mr. Speaker also acquainted the House, That, in Obedience to the Commands of this House of the 6th Day of April last, he had, by Letter to the Colonel, or other Commanding Officer of each of the respective Corps of Militia which have been embodied in Great Britain and Ireland during the Course of the War, signified the Resolutions of this House ': — That the Thanksof this House, be given to the Officers of the said Corps of Militia, for the lcasonable and meritorious Services they have rendered to their King and Country: And that this House doth highly approve of, and acknowledge, the Services of the Non-commissioned Officers and Men of the said Corps of Militia; and that the same be communicated to them by the Colonels, or Commanding Officers of the several Corps, who are desired to thank 'them for their meritorious Conduct:

And that he had received An fivers by Letters from moll of the said Colonels, or other Commanding Officers, tiefiring him to make their grateful Acknowledgment for the great Honour done the Militia, by the Notice which this House has been pleased to take of their Endeavours to lerve their King and Country,

Mr. Speaker likewise acquainted the House, That, in Obedience to the Commands of this House of the 6th Day of April lall, he had by Letter to His Majesty's Lieutenant of each County, Riding, and Place, in Great Britain, and to his Excellency the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, signified the Resolutions of this House: — That the Thanks of this House be given to the Officers of the several Coqis of Yeomanry and Volunteer Cavalry, and Infantry, and of the Sea Fencibles, which have been formed in Great Britain and Ireland during the Course of the War, lor the seasonable and eminent Services they have rendered to their King and Country: And that this House doth highly approve of, and acknowledge, the Services of the Non-commissioned Officers and Men of the said several Corps; and that the same be communicated to them by the Colonels, and other Commanding Officers of the several Corps, who are defiled to thank them for their meritorious Conduct:

And that he had received Answers by Letters from moll of the said Lieutenants, and from his Excellency the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, desiring him to make the grdteful Acknowledgments of the said several Corps for the Honour done to them by the Notice which this House has been pleased to take of their Services and Conduct.

That, by the Act, passed to amend in the 39th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for nXa. rendering more commodious, and for better regulating,

the Port of London, certain Rates are directed to be paid to the Directors of the f India Dock Company by the Owners of Ships or Vessels using such Docks, as a Satis-3

faction for (atnongst other Things) the Cooperage, and Hoops and Nails, which the Cargoes thereof may require in the unlading thereof; and certain other Rates are to be paid by the Owners or Consignees of such Goods to such Directors, in Satisfaction for (amongst other Things) such Cooperage as the same may respectively want alter being unshipped; and that the Cooperage to such Goods in the unlading thereof, and after the same have been unshipped, is Part of the Trade of the Petitioners, and of which they will be deprived by the Provisions of the said Act; and Doubts have been entertained whether the same of the Petitioners is included in the Words of the Section of the said Act, authorizing certain Persons therein named to claim Compensations for the Injury, Loss, or Damage, they may suffer or sustain by the Works in the said Act mentioned; and that a Bill is now depending in the House, to alter and amend the said Act, so far as relates to the Concerns of the West India Dock Company thereby established; and, in order to remove the Doubts aforesaid, and to entitle the Petitioners to claim Indemnity, they hope that a Clause may be inserted in the said Bill to grant them Liberty to claim Compensation for such Injury as they may suffer in their Trade and Occupation, in consequence of the Clause referred to in the said Act: And therefore praying, That they may be heard upon the Premises, by themselves, their Counsel, and Agents, before the Committee, upon the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by them-lelves, their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Mr. Henry Alexander reported from the Committee, appointed to enquire what Laws are expired, or near ex-, piring, and to report their Opinion, from Time to Time, to the House, which of them are fit to be revived, continued, or made perpetual; That the Committee had made a further Enquiry, and had come to several other Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 39th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to revive and continue, until the End of the next Session of Parliament, " an Act, made in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of '* His present Majesty, to continue and amend an Act, " made in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the more effectual Encouragement of the British Fifieries; and to 4< amend an Act, made in the Twenty-sixth Year of the " Reign of His present Majesty, for extending the " Fisheries, and improving the Sea Coasts of this K.ingdom," which was amended and continued by an Act, of the 39th and 40th Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, and revived, amended, and continued, by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, until the 5th Day of April 1802, is expired, and fit to be revived and continued, with Amendments.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 6th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to prohibit the Importation of Foreign Wrought Silks and Velvets, fora " limited Time; and for preventing unlawful Combinations of Workmen employed in the SilkManufacture," which was to continue in Force for the Term of Five Years from the 14th Day of 1766, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by (cveral subsequent Acts, made in the 1 ithand 17th Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, was further continued until the 14th Day of June 1782, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which Act, so far as relates to the prohibiting the Importation of Foreign Wrought Silks and Velvets, was, by Three Acts, made in the 22d, 29th, and 35th Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, further continued until the 14th Day of June 1802, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

The said Resolutions being read a Second Time;

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, humbly to represent to His Majesty, that, in Consideration of the great Importance of preventing the Dangers and Mischiefs which must arise from the excessive Increase of the Importation of Negroes from Africa, if such Importation should be permitted. Without Restriction, into the Island of Trinidad; and for the Purpose of avoiding any Colour or Pretext, by reason of new Grants, to obstruct hereafter any Regulations which, to the Wisdom of Parliament, may, after due In-vefligation and Deliberation, seem expedient; His Majesty's faithful Commons humbly request His Majesty, that He will not authorize any Grants or Sales of new Lands in the Island of Trinidad without express Condition (under Penalty of forfeiting and making void such Grants or Sales) that no Negro to be thenceforth imported from Africa shall be employed on the said Lands, until Opportunity shall have been afforded to Parliament to make such Provision as the Circumstances of the same may be found to require, for the Prohibition, Limitation, or Regulation, of the Importation of Negroes from Africa into the said IslandThat His Majesty will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that there shall be laid before this House, in the next Session of Parliament, an Account of any such Conditional Grapts and Sales, as may have been made in the Interval; and of the Means which have been employed, or provided, for enforcing the due Observation and Performance of the said Condition; and that His Majesty will be graciously pleased further to direct, that there ljta.ll be laid before this House, so soon as the same can be prepared, such Plan of Regulations as to His Majesty's Government may appear most advilable, for promoting the Cultivation or Improvement of the Island of Trinidad, in the Manner the lead likely to interfere with the Wilh expressed by this House for the gradual Diminution, and ultimate Termination, of the African Slave Trade, and the most conducive to the Stability and Security of the

The Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Report on Mr. Henry Alexander, according to Order, reported Letters to and ^l0m die Committee of the whole House, to whom it from France, was referred to consider of so much of certain Acts, &c* made in the 9th Year of the Reign of Queen , and

in the last Session of Parliament, as relate to the Pollage of Letters to and from France, or the Batavian Republic, from and to London; and who were inltrudted to consider of exempting from the Duty of Tonnage, granted by an Act of this present Session of Parliament, any Ships or Vessels employed by the Republic of France to convey the Mails of Letters between the Two Countries, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's 'Fable: Where the same were read; and are as follow-cth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rates of Pollage payable on the Conveyance of Letters and Packets to or from France, or the Batavian Republic, from or to , do cease and de-

termine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for the Conveyance of all Letters and Packets sent by the Poll to or from France from or to London, for every Single Letter Ten Pence; for every Double Letter One Shilling and Eight Pence; for every Treble Letter Two Shillings and Sixpence; and for every Ounce in Weight Three Shillings and Four Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be charged for the Conveyance of all Letters and Packets sent by the Poll to or from the Batavian Republic from or to London, for every Single Letter One Shilling; for every Double Letter Two Shillings; for every Treble Letter Three Shillings; and for every Ounce in Weight Four Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Duty whatever shall be payable on the Tonnage of any Ships or Vessels employed in conveying the Mails ot letters from France to Great Britain.

The laid Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Mr. Alderman Curtis reported from the Committee, Report on to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, ^'aing'eftai-and Commons of the City of London, in Common Coun- blishing of cil assembled; and also, the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Grand Junction Canal, were severally referred; That the Committee had heard Counsel in Support of the said Petitions; and had also examined the Matters contained in the said Petitions, and had come to several Resolutions thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, from the Evidence produced to them, That the Corporation of the City of London have not established or exercised any Jurisdiction, at any Time, over the Lands which now belong to the Grand Junction Canal Company at Paddington.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

A Petition of Peter Levcrfage, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners perceiving by an Act, passed in the present Session of Parliament, that no Maltster or Maker of Malt shall wet any Grain making into Malt, after taken out of the Cistern, until the End of Twelve Days, are apprehensive such Regulation will be prejudicial to the proper making of Malt: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to grant such Relief as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the House, an Account of the Money granted for the Year 1800, examined and passed by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer; and that, in Consideration of the various Expences to which the Establishments in Africa are fub-ject having risen to a very great Degree, and the Prices of the Articles necessary for the Maintenance thereof having so much advanced, that it was found impossible to keep the Forts in any tolerable Degree of Security with the former Annual Supply, the same Grant not producing at present much more than One Half of what it formerly yielded, the House granted to the Petitioners, in the last Session, the Sum of £. 20,000; and that the same Inconveniencies still exist in their full Force: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and grant such adequate Sum, for the effectual permanent Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, as shall seem meet.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That there be charged upon every Insurance, where the Premium actually given, or contracted for, shall not exceed the Rate of Twenty Shillings for every f. 100, or any fractional Part of f. 100 insured, the like Duties as

are payable by the said Acts upon Insurances where the Premium actually given, or contracted for, shall not exceed the Rate of Ten Shillings/wr Centum on the Sum in lured.

Resolved., That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Two Shillings and Sixpence, Part of the Duty of Three Shillings and Sixpence, and also the additional Duty of One Shilling, which were granted on Sea Insurances made in Ireland, by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, shall not be charged on any Insurance of Ships or Merchandize for any Voyage to or from any Part of the United Kingdom, or the Wands of Guernsey, Jersey, Alderney, Sark, or Man.

The Commons agree to the Eight next Amendments made by your Lordships,

" or have been taken:" For the same Reason for which they disagree to the Amendment, Press 83. 1.4.

Because it does not seem expedient to give other or further Powers than those described in the Clause as sent from this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is iuft and equitable that Compensation should be made to the several Counties and Places in who may incur any Expence in consequence of the - Discharge of certain Militia Men, whenever it shall

appear, from the Tenor of the several Attentions, that any of the Men so discharged were legally bound to serve for a further Period than that at which they were, or may hereafter be, so severally discharged.

Re/o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Chief Governor or Chief Governors of Ireland, for the Time being, should be authorized to order and direct, from Time to Time, such Sum or Sums of Money as may appear to him or them necessary for reimbursing to the several Counties and Places in Ireland the Expences which such Counties and Places may incur, in certain Cafes, in consequence of discharging certain Militia Men, respecting the Periods of whole Service Doubts have been entertained, to be paid to the Clerk of the Peace for such Counties and Places, to be by him accounted for, by any of the Collectors of His Majesty's Revenue out of any Public Monies in their Hands, or out of any of the Aids or Supplies which shall be granted to His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors; and every Sum so paid by any Collector shall be allowed to every such Collector in his Accounts.

Henry Alexander, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of so much of an Act, made in this present Session of Parliament, as relates to the Duty on Spermaceti Oil, and to Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, the Produce of the Colonies and Plantations in America, re I to red to the French and Batavian Republics by the late Treaty of Peace, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and arc as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duty, granted by any Act of this Session of Parliament, on Spermaceti Oil, shall cease and 'determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pounds Three Shillings and Ten rcncc be charged upon every Ton, containing Two hundred and Fifty-two Gallons of Spermaceti Oil, imported into Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Goods, Warcs, and Merchandize, the Produce of, and imported directly into this Kingdom, from any of the Colonies and Plantations in America, restored to the French and Batavian Republics by the late Treaty of Peace, be permitted, for a Time to be limited, to be landed, on Payment of the like Duties as if imported from any British Colony or Plantation in America.

ration of A Petition of the uncertificated Bankrupts confined in KinkrapM^n His Majesty's Prison of the Fleet, was presented to the ttie Fleet, for House, and read; Setting forth, That, through great Relief! Losses in Trade, and other unavoidable Misfortunes, Commissions of Bankruptcy have been issued against the Petitioners; and, notwithstanding the y have duly and driftly complied with the Bankrupt Laws, they have l»ot been able to procure the Signatures of forrte of their Creditors, the said Laws absolutely requiring the Signatures of Four-Fifths in Number and Value of i'uch Creditors, who shall have proved their Debts under the Commission, to the Completion of the Bankrupt's Certificate; and that some of their Creditors have offered to sign the Certificates of the Petitioners, provided their Friends would pay them certain Compositions, in Discharge of the Debts they have proved against the said Bankrupts Estates; but as the Payment of any. Composition whatever, on Behalf of the Bankrupt, would render his Certificate null and void, no Composition for such Purpose can possibly be made; and that, in consequence of the Petitioners not having been able to get their Certificates signed as the Law directs, they have been arrested for Debts contracted previous to their respective Commissions being issued, and in Discharge of their Bail, have been surrendered to the Fleet Prifdn;

and that the Petitioners have surrendered the Whole of

their Property and Effects, and, in consequence of being immured within the Walls of a Prison, are now, with' their Wives and Families, in the greatest Distress j and-that, as the Legislature is pleased to afford Relief to unJ certificated Bankrupts in the Petitioners hope the

House will, at the same Time, commiserate their unhappy Situation, so that they may be united in the same Act. Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.
