Petitionefthe A Petition was presented to the Hgufe, and read; Desc'endant* Setting forth. That the there-undersigned, immediate of his Hish- Descendants of his late Highncls IVallajah Behauder, &c. Bch3uder'^ah &c- and Brothers of his Highness Omdut ul &c.

au er‘ late Newaubs of the Car, approach the House with heart-felt Grief and Affliction: — That they have not been accustomed, from Birth and Situation, to seek and implore Assistance at a Foreign Hand, and are wholly unacquainted with the Language of Petition; and would therefore hope, that the House will impute any Failure in Form or Respect, if any should be conceived, to their utter Want of Knowledge in the Customs and Manners which the House may chance to have ordained: But they feel allured, that the House will not turn afide from any Subject of just Complaint, in whatever Form or whatever Language it present itself: — That it is with Confidence, therefore, that they approach, and make known those Sufferings, which have weighed them down to the Earth; for they have to acquaint the House, that they cannot but consider and lament the late unfortu-

nate Succession to the Mufnud of the Carnatic, dictated by the Government of Fort Saint George, by the Sword of the East India Company, as the Destruction of the Dc-

feent of their ancient and honourable Family, a Degradation of the Dignity of the Sovereignty, an Abuse of the Ordinations of the Law, and a Sacrifice of the Wights of the People: — That they enjoyed indeed an Instant Happiness in contemplating the Acccfiion of a Prince de-Icended from the Loins of their much beloved and highly honoured Brother, and appointed by the Will of his Royal Father, as of Right, to the Mufnud of his Predecessors; but had scarcely Time to congratulate themselves and his People on the Event, before they had the Misery to behold him call from his Throne, placed amongst the lowed of his Subjects, and his hereditary Empire and Dominions conveyed, by the Hand of an unlawful Successor, as a Largess to those avho had forced him, with a Dilregard of every Principle of Right and of humaniled Policy, into an unbidden Situation: — by which flagrant Act of Injustice, they have humbly to represent to the House, that the real and indisputable Heir to the Empire has been circumvented, and they, the Descendants from a Line of Sovereigns, barred for ever, both in themselves and Progeny, from the Enjoyment of their hereditary Honours and Dignities, have been reduced into a State of Dependency on that Power which has occasioned this mighty and incomparable Mischief, and are delivered into the Custody of him, who. with (b little Consideration and Remorse, has already sacrificed the Rights, and may eventually devote the Persons, of his Kind: — They therefore implore and beseech the House (for, alas!, they have no other Hope) to enquire into, and consider their distressed Condition, and afford them that Relief, which the House, in its Wisdom and Justice, shall think fit: And they the Subscribers, and a grateful People, shall ever pray for the long Continuation of the Prosperity and Honours of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And then the House adjourned till To-morrotV Morning, Ten of the Clock.

1r. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for raising the Sum of Five Millions by Loans or Exchequer Bills, for the Service of Great Britain, for the Year One thousand Eight hundred and Three; without any Amendment: And also, *

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing the Duties granted by an Act, made in this Session of Parliament, on Spermaceti Oil, Blubber, Train Oil, Fish Oil, or Oil of Seals, and granting other Duties in lieu thereof; for repealing the Duties granted by the said Act on Linen Yarn made of Flax, and on Goods,

Wares, dr Merchandize, imported by the East India Company, and exported from the Warehouse in which the same shall have been secured; for exempting Stone, the Produce of Guernsey, Jersey, Alderney, Sark, or Man, from Duty; and for permitting Merchandize, the Produce of any of the Colonies ceded to the French and Batavian Republics, to be imported for Three Years from the passing of this Act, upon Payment of certain Duties; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enlarging the Time for which Horses may be let to Hire without being subject to any Annual Duty; for explaining and amending several Acts relating to the Duties on Horses, Servants, and Carriages; and for authorizing the Allowance in the Accounts of the Receivers General of the several Sums advanced by them in pursuance of the Acts for raising a Provisional Force of Cavalry, and not reimbursed to them, by Assessment; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for authorizing, and rendering valid, the Discharge of certain Militia Men in Ireland, and for giving Indemnity to the several Counties and Places in Ireland which may incur any Expence in consequence of the Discharge of certain Militia Men; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to authorize the Commissioners of Excise to order the Restoration of Exciseable Goods seized or detained by Officers of Excise; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing certain Duties on Paper, Pasteboards, Mill-boards, Scaleboards, and Glazed Paper, imported into, pr made in, Great Britain, and for granting other Duties in lieu thereof; without any Amendment: And

also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, several Acts of the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Years of the Reign of King Charles the Second, and of the Seventh and Thirty-fifth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, relating to the Navigation of the River Itchin, in the County of Southampton; without any Amendment.

AMeffage by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts, agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned}

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commissiont afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and allb empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Kent, His Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland, His Royal Highness the Duke of SuJJ'ex, His Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Afient to the said Bills; and that the Lord High Chancellor, the Lord Pelham, and the Lord Walsingham, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

Answers to The Lord Arden reported to the House, That their

Addresses. Address of Thursday last (humbly to lay before His Majesty a Copy of the Report which was made from the Committee, who were appointed to consider of a Plan to be submitted to His Majesty, for providing additional Committee Rooms and Offices for the Use of this I louse; and to request His Majesty, that He would be graciously pleased to give Directions for carrying into Effect the Alterations and Improvements therein described; and to assure His Majesty, that this House will make good the Expence attending the fame) had been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that He will give Directions as desired by the said Address.

The Lord Arden also reported to the House, That - their Address of Thursday last (humbly to represent to His Majesty, that it appears to this House, that Doctor James Carmichael Smyth, having long directed his Attention to the most effectual Means of preventing Infection, at length discovered and introduced the Use of his Nitric Fumigation, and established its Efficacy, in preventing the Communication of Contagion; that the Use of the said Fumigation has already been attended with the most beneficial Effects, especially in His Majesty's Naval and Military Hospitals, and in Transports and Ships of War; and that it may justly be expected to be hereafter productive of the most extensive Advantages, particularly to His Majesty's Fleets and Armies; and humbly befecching His Majesty, that, in Consideration of the Merit of the said Discovery and Application, His Majesty will be graciously pleased to direct a Sum, not exceeding £. 5,000, to be advanced to the said ‘ Doctor James Carmichael Smyth; and to assure His Majesty, that this House will make good the fame) had been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that He will give Directions as desired by the said Address.

The Lord Arden also reported to the House, That their Address of Yesterday (that His Majesty would be graciously pleased to confer some Dignity in the Church upon the Reverend Mr. John , Chaplain to this House) had been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this I louse, that He will confer some Dignity in the Church upon the Reverend Mr. John Barton, as is desired.

The Lord Arden likewise reported to the House, That their several other Addresses of Yesterday had been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that He will give Directions as desired by the said Addresses.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Ten of the Clock.

A Message from His Majesty, by Sir Francis Mo/yneux, Gentleman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty; where His Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills following; viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty certain Sums of Money out of the respective Consolidated Funds of Great Britain and Ireland; for applying certain Monies therein mentioned for the Service of the Year One thousand Eight hundred and Two; and for further appropriating the Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament:

An Act for granting to His Majesty certain additional Duties on Goods imported into, and exported from, Ireland:

An Act for defraying the Charge of the Pay of the Milit ia of Ireland, until the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Eight hundred and Three; and for holding Courts Martial on Serjeant Majors, Serjeants, Corporals, and Drummers, for Offences committed during the Time such Militia shall not be embodied:

An Act to suppress certain Games and Lotteries not authorized by Law.

After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a most Gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Public Business being concluded, I think it proper to dole this Session of Parliament.

During a long and laborious Attendance, you ha?e invariably manifested the just Sense you entertain of the great Trust committed to your Charge. The Objects of your Deliberations have been unusually numerous and important; and I derive the utmost Satisfaction from the Conviction, that the Wisdom of your Proceedings will be fully proved by their Effects, in promoting the belt Interests of My People throughout every Part of My Dominions.

Gentlemen of the House of Commonn,

The ample Provision you have made lor the various Branches of the Public Service demands My warmest Acknowledgments; and My particular Thanks are due for the Liberality which you have shewn in exonerating 3 My

Account of Balances of Land Revenue, presented.

Royal Assent to Bills.

His Majesty Speech.

42 Geo. ill. 28° Junii.

My Civil Government and Household from the Debt with which they were unavoidably burthened.

Whild I regret the Amount of the Supplies which Circumstances have rendered necessary, it is a Relief to Me to contemplate the State of Our Manufactures, Commerce, and Revenue, which afford the most decisive and gratifying Proofs of the Abundance of Our internal Resources, and of the growing Prosperity of the Country.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

As I think it expedient that the Election of a new Parliament should take place without Delay, it is My Intention, forthwith, to give Directions for dissolving the present, and for calling a new Parliament.

In communicating to you this Intention, I cannot suppress those Sentiments of entire Approbation with which I rellect upon every Part of your Conduct since I first met you in this Place. The unexampled Difficulties of our Situation required the utmost Efforts of that Wisdom and Fortitude which you so eminently d if-played in contending with them, and by which they have been so happily l'urmounted. From your judicious and salutary Measures during the lad Year, My People derived all the Relief which could be afforded under one of the fevered Dispensations of Providence; and it was by the Spirit and Determination which uniformly

animated your Councils, aided by the unprecedented Exertions of My Fleets and Armies, and the zealous and cordial Co-operation of My People, that I was enabled to prosecute with Succcfs, and terminate with Honour the long and arduous Conted in which We have been engaged.

The same Sense of public Duty, the same Solicitude for the Welfare of your Country, will now, in your individual Characters, induce you to encourage, by all the Means in your Power, the Cultivation and Improvement of the Advantages of Peace.

My Endeavours will never be wanting to preserve the Blessings by whiefc We are so eminently distinguished, and to prove that the Prosperity and Happiness of all Clafies of My faithful Subjects are the Objects which are always the neared to My Heart.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty's Command, laid.

Parliament

prorogued.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

' It is His Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to Tuesday the 17th Day of August next, to be then here holden; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday the 17th Day of August next.

Appendix* TRANSLATION of Convention between Hi« Britaknic Majiitt and the Emperor of Russia, signed at St. Peters-(No. I.) burgh, the -fr June 1801.

c — - In the Name of the Most Holy and Undivided Trinity.

THE mutual Desire of His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and of his Majesty the Emperor of all the Ruflias, being not only to come to an Under-Banding between themselves with respect to the Differences which have lately interrupted the good Understanding and friendly Relations which subsisted between the Two Spates; but also to prevent, by frank and precise Explanations upon the Navigation of their respective Subjects, the Renewal of similar Altercations and Troubles which might be the Confluence of them; and the common Object of the Solicitude of their said Majrftie being to settle, as soon as can be done, an equitable Arrangement of those Differences, and an invariable Determination of their Principles upon the Rights of Neutrality, in their Application to their respective Monarchies, in order to unite more closely the Ties of Priendship and good Intercourse, of which they acknowledge the Utility and the Benefits, have named and chosen for their Plenipotentiaries; w/*. His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, Alleyne Lord Baron Saint Helens, His said Majesty's Privy Counsellor, and His Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to his Majesty the Emperor of all the Ruflias; and his Majesty the Emperor of all the Ruflias, the Sieur Nikita Count de Panin, his Privy Counsellor, Minister of State for the Department of Foreign Affairs, present Chamberlain, Knight Grand Croft of the Orders of Saint Alexander Newflcy, and of Saint Anne of the First Class, of that of Saint Ferdinand, and of Merit, of the Red Eagle, and of Saint Lazarus; who, after having communicated their respective full Powers, and found them in good and due Form, have agreed upon the following Points and Articles:

ARTICLE L There (Ball be hereafter between His Britannic Majesty and his Imperial Majesty of all the Ruflias, their Subjects, the States and Countries under their Dominion, good and unalterable Friendftiip and Understanding; and all die political, commercial, and other Relations of common Utility between the respective Subjects, shall subsist as formerly, without their being disturbed or troubled in any Manner whatever.

ARTICLE II.

His Britannic Majesty and the Emperor of all the Ruflias declare, that they will watch over the most rigorous Execution of the Prohibitions against the Trade of Contraband of their Subjects with the Enemies of either of the High Contracting Parties.

ARTICLE HI.

His Britannic Majesty and his Imperial Majesty of all the Ruflias having resolved to place, under a fufijeieut Safeguard, the Free-dorn of Commerce, and Navigation of their Subjects, in case One of them shall be at War, whilst the other shall be Neuter, have agreed:

I*. That the Ships of the Neutral Power may navigate freely to the Ports, and upon the Cosfts of the Nations at War.

2*°. That the Effects embarked on board Neutral Ships shall be free, with the Exception of Contraband of War, and of Enemy's Property; and it is agreed not to comprize, in the Numbet of the VOL. 57.

latter, the Merchandize of the Produce, Growth, or Manufacture of the Countries at War, which should have been acquired by the Subjects of the Neutral Power, and should lie transported for their Account, which Merchandize cannot be accepted in any same from the Freedom granted to the Flag of the said Power. v

3Ii#. That, in order to avoid all Equivocation and Misunder-standing of what ought to be considered as Contraband of War, His Britannic Majesty, and his Imperial Majesty of all the Ruflias declare, conformably to the nth Article of the Treaty of Commerce concluded between the Two Crowns, on the February 1797, That they acknowledge as such the following Objects only; viz. Cannons, Mortars, Fire Arms, Pistols, Bombs, Grenades, Balls, Bullets, Firelocks, Flints, Matches, Gunpowder, Saltpetre, Sulphur, Cuiraffes, Pikes, Swords, Sword Belts, Knapsacks, SaddLs, and Bridles, excepting, how ever, the Quantity 01 the said Articles which may be necessary for the Defence of the Ship, and of those who compose the Crew; and all other Articles whatever, not enumerated here, shall not be reputed Warlike and Naval Stores, nor be subject to Confiscation, and of course shall pass freely, without being subjected to the smallest Difficulty, unless they be considered Enemy's Property in the Sense above specified. It is also agreed that, that which is stipulated in the present Article shall not be prejudicial to the particular Stipulations of one or the other Crown with other Powers, by which Objects of a similar Kind should be reserved, prohibited, or permitted.

4t0. That, in order to determine what characterifes a blockaded Port, that Denomination is given only to a Port where there is, by the Dispositions of the Power which attacks it with Ships stationary, or sufficiently near, an evident Danger in entering.

5to. That the Ships of the Neutral Power shall not be (lopped but upon just Causes and evident Facts; that they be tried without Delay; and that the Proceeding be always uniform, prompt, and legal.

In order the better to insure the RespeCi due to these Stipulations, dilated by the sincere Desire of conciliating every Imereft, and to give a new Proof of their Uprightness and Love of Justice, the High Contracting Parties enter here into the most formal Engagement to renew the severest Prohibitions to their Captains, whether of Ships of War, or Merchantmen, to take, keep, or conceal, on board their Ships, any of the Objects which, in the Terms of the present Convention, may be reputed Contraband, and respectively to take Care of the Execution of the Order* which they shall have pubiiftied in their Admiralties, and wherever it shall be necessary.

ARTICLE IV.

The Two High Contracting Parties, wishing % Hb to prevent all Subject of Diffension in future, by limiting the Right of Search of Merchant Ships going under Convoy to those Cafes only in which the Belligerent Power might experience a real Prejudice by the Abuse of the Neutral Flag, have agreed,

I*. That the Right of searching Merchant Ships belonging to the Subjects of One of the Contracting Parries, and navigating under Convoy of a Ship of War of the said Power, shall only be exercised by Ships of War of the Belligerent Parry, and shall never extend to Letters of Marque, Privateers, or other Vefllls, which do not belong to the Royal or Imperial f leet of their Majesties, but which their Subjects shall have fitted out for War.

a*0. That the Proprietors of all Merchant Ships, belonging to the Subjects of One of the Contracting Sovereigns, which shall be destined to fail under Convoy of a Ship of War, shall be

quired, before they receive their Sailing Orders, to produce to the Commander of the Convoy their Passports and Certificates, or Sea Letters, in the Form annexed to the present Treaty.

3*^. That when such Ship of War, having under Convoy Merchant Ships, shall be met with by a Ship or Ships of War of the other Contracting Party, who shall then be in a State of War, in order to avoid all Disorder, they shall keep out of Cannot Shot, unless the State of the Sea, or the Place of Meeting, render a nearer Approach necessary; and the Commander of the Ship of the Belligerent Power shall fend a Boat on board the Convoy, where they shall proceed reciprocally to the Verification of the Papers and Certificates that are to prove on one Part, that the Ship of War is authorized to take under its Escort such or such Merchant Ships of its Nation, laden with such a Cargo, and for such a Port; on the other Part, that the Ship of War of the Belligerent Party belongs to the Royal or Imperial Fleet of their Majesties.

4t % . This Verification made, there shall be no Pretence for any Search, if the Papers are found in Form, and if there exists no good Motive for Suspicion. In the contrary Cafe, the Commander of the Neutral Ship of War (being duly required thereto by the Commanderof the Ship or Ships of War of the Belligerent Power) is to bring to, and detain his Convoy during the Time necessary for the Search of the Ships which compose it, and he shall have the Faculty of naming and delegating One or more Officers to assist at the Search of the said Ships, which shall be done in his Presence on board each Merchant Ship, conjointly with One or more Officers appointed by the Commander of the Ship of the Belligerent Party.

If it happens that the Commander of the Ship or Ships of the Power at War, having examined the Papers found on board, and having interrogated the Matter and Crew of the Ship, shall fee just and sufficient Reason to detain the Merchant Ship, in order to proceed to an ulterior Search, he shall notify such Intention to the Commander of the Convoy, who shall have the Power to order an Officer to remain on board the Ship thus detained, and to attitt at the Examination of the Cause of her Detention. The Merchant Ships shall be carried immediately to the neared and most convenient Port belonging to the Belligerent Power, and the ulterior Search shall be carried on with all possible Diligence.

ARTICLE V.

It is in like Manner agreed, that if any Merchant Ship, thus convoyed, should be detained without just and sufficient Cause, the Commander of the Ship or Ships of War of the Belligerent Power shall not only be bound to make to the Owners of the Ship and of the Cargo a full and perfect Compenffition for all the Lottes, Expences, Damages, and Costs, occasioned by such a Detention, but shall moreover undergo an ulterior Punishment for every Ad of Violence or other Fault which he may have committed, according as the Nature of the same may require. On the other Hand, the Convoying Ship shall not be permitted, under any Pretext whatsoever, to refill by Force the Detention of the Merchant Ship or Ships of War of the Belligerent Power; an Obligation to which the Commander of a Ship of War with Convoy is not bound to observe towards Letters of Marque and Privateers.

ARTICLE VI.

The High Contracting Parties shall give precise and efficacious Orders, that the Judgments upon Prizes made at Sea shall be conformable with the Rules of the most exact Justice and Equity; that they shall be given by Judges above Suspicion, and who shall not be interested in the Affair in question. The Government of the respective States shall take care that the said Decisions shall be speedily and duly executed, according to the Forms prescribed: and, in case of an unfounded Detention, or other Contravention to the Regulations stipulated by the present Article, the Owners of such Ship and Cargo shall be allowed Damages proportioned to the Loss occasioned thereby. The Rules to observe for these Damages, and for the same of unfounded Detention, as also the Principles to follow for the Purpose of accelerating the Process, shall be the Matter of Additional Articles, which the Contracting Parties agree to settle between them, and which shall have the same Force and Validity as if they were inferred in the present Act. For this Efted, their Britanuic and Imperial Majestics mutually engage to put their Hand to the salutary Work which may Icrve for the Completion of theie Stipulations, and to communicate to each other, without Delay, the Views which may be fuggetted' 4

to them by their equal Solicitude to prevent the lead Grounds for Dispute in future.

ARTICLE VII.

To obviate all the Inconveniencies which may arise from the bad Faith of those who avail themselves of the Flag of a Nation without belonging to it, it is agreed to establish, for an invariable Rule, that any Vessel whatever, in order to be considered as the Property of the Country the Flag of which it carries, mutt have on board the Captain of the Ship, and One Half of the Crew, of the People of that Country, and the Papers and Passports in due and perfect Form; but every Vessel which shall not observe this Rule, and which shall infringe the Ordinances published on that Head, shall lose all Rights to the Protection of the Contracting Powers.

ARTICLE VIII.

The Principles and Measures adopted by the present Act shall be alike applicable to all the Maritime Wars in which One of the Two Powers may be engaged, whilll the other remains neutral. These Stipulations shall in consequence be regarded as permanent, and shall serve for a constant Rule to the Contracting Powers ia Matters of Commerce and Navigation.

ARTICLE IX.

His Majesty the King of Denmark, and his Majesty the King of Sweden, shall be immediately invited by his Imperial Majesty, in the Name of the Two Contracting Parties, to accede to the present Convention, and at the same Time to renew and confirm their respective Treaties of Commerce with His Britannic Majesty; and His said Majesty engages, by Acts which shall have established that Agreement, to render and restore to each of these Powers all the Prizes that have been taken from them, as well as the Territories and Countries under their Dominion, w'hich have been conquered by the Arms of His Britannic Majesty since the Rupture, in the State in which those Possessions were found at the Period at which the Troops of His Britannic Majesty entered them. The Orders of His said Majesty, for the Restitution of those Prizes and Conquests, shall be immediately expedited after the Exthange of the Ratifications'of the Acts by which Sweden and Denmark shall accede to the present Treaty.

ARTICLE X.

The present Convention shall be ratified by the Two Contracting Parties, and the Ratifications exchanged at St. Petersburgh in the Space of Two Months at furthest, from the Day of the Signature.

In Faith of which the respective Plenipotentiaries have caused to be made Two Copies thereof, perfectly similar, signed with their Hands; and have caused the Seal of their Arms to be affixed thereto.

Done at Saint Petersburgh, the June One thousand Eight hundred and One.

The pure and mignanimous Intentions of his Majesty the Emperor of all the Ruffias having already induced him to restore the Vessels and Goods of British Subjects, which had been fe-questered in Russia, his said Majesty confirms that Dispofidon in its whole Extent; and His Britannic Majesty engages Himself also to give immediate Orders for taking off ail Sequestration laid upon the Russian, Danish, and Swedish Properties, detained in English Ports; and to prove tlil! more His fir.cere Desire to terminate amicably the Differences which have arisen between Great Britain and the Northern Courts, and in order that no new Incident may throw Obllacles in the Way of this salutary Work, His Britannic Majesty binds Himself to give Orders to the Commanders of His Forces by Land and Sea, that the Armistice, now subsisting with the Courts of Denmark and Sweden, shall be prolonged for a Term of Three Months, from the Date of this Dav; and his Majesty the Emperor of all the Rufiias, guided by the same Motive s, undertakes, in the Name of his Allies, to have this A.miitice maintained during the said Term.

This Separate Article shall have the same Force and Validity, as if it were inserted Word for Word in the Treaty signed this Day; and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged at the same Time.

COPY of Preliminary Articles of Peace between His Majesty and the French Republic; signed at London the 1 ft of October 1801.

His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and I reland, and the First Confu! of the French Republic, in the Name of the French People, being animated with an equal Desire of putting an End to the Calamities ofp. destructive War, and of re-establishing Union and good Uudcrstanding between the Two Countries, have named for this Purpose; namely. His Britannic Majesty, the Right honourable Robert Banks Jenkinson, commonly called Lord Hawkesbury, One of His Britannic Majesty's Most honourable Privy Council, and His Principal Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs; and the First Consul of the French Republic, in the Name of the French People, Citizen Lewis William Otto, Commissary for the Exchange of French Prisoners in England; who, after having duly communicated to each other their full Powers, in good Form, have agreed on the following Preliminary Articles:

ARTICLE I.

As soon as the Preliminaries shall be signed and ratified, sincere Friendship shall be re-established between His Britannic Majesty and the French Republic, by Sea and by Land, in all Parts of the World; and in order that all Hostilities may cease immediately between the Two Powers, and between them and their Allies respectively, the necessary Instructions shall be sent, with the ut-moil Dispatch, to the Commanders of the Sea and Land Forces of the respective States; and each of the Contracting Parties engages to grant Passports, and every Facility requisite to accelerate the Arrival and ensure the Execution of these Orders. It is farther agreed, That all Conquests which may hare been made by either of the Contracting Parties from the otTier, or from their respective Allies, subsequently to the Ratification of the present Preliminaries, shall be considered as of no Effect, and shall be faithfully comprehended in the Restitutions to be made after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty.

ARTICLE II.

His Britannic Majesty shall restore to the French Republic and her Allies; namely, to his Catholic Majesty, and to the Batavian Republic, all the Possessions and Colonies occupied or conquered by the English Forces in the Course of the present War, with the Exception of the I Hand of Trinidad, and the Dutch Pofff ffions in the Istand of Ceylon; of which Island and Possessions His Britannic Majesty reserves to Himself the full and entire Sovereignty.

ARTICLE III.

The Port of the Cape of Good Hope shall be open to the Commerce and Navigation of the Two Contracting Parties, who shall enjoy therein the same Advantages.

ARTICLE IV.

The Island of Malta, with its Dependencies, shall be evacuated by the Troops of His Britannic Majesty, and restored to the Order of St. John of Jerusalem. For the Purpose of rendering this Istand completely independent of either of the Two Contracting Parties, it shall be placed under the Guarantee and Protection of a Third Power, to be agreed upon in the Definitive Treaty.

ARTICLE V.

Egypt Hull be redored to the Sublime Porte, whole Territories and Possessions shall be preferred entire, such as they existed previously to the present War.

ARTICLE VL

The Territories and Possessions of her Mod Faithful Majesty shall likewise be preserved entire.

ARTICLE VII.

The French Forces shall evacuate the Kingdom of Naples and the Roman Territory. The English Forces shall in like Manner evacuate Porto Ferrajo; and, generally, all the Ports and Idands which they may occupy in the Mediterranean or in the Adriatic.

ARTICLE VIII.

The Republic of the Seven Idands shall be acknowledged by the French Republic.

ARTICLE IX.

The Evacuations, Cedions, and Reditutions, (lipulated for by the present Preliminary Articles, shall take place in Europe within One Month; in the Continent and Seas of America and of Africa, within Three Months; and in the Continent and Seas of Alia, within Six Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty.

ARTICLE X.

The Prisoners made respectively shall, immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications of the Definitive Treaty, all be redored, and without Ran Com, on paying reciprocally the Debts which they may have individually con traded. Discussions having arisen respecting the Payment for the Maintenance of Prisoners of War, the Contracting Powers reserve this Question to be settled ky the Definitive Treaty, according to the Law of Nations, and in Conformity to established Usage.

A R T I C L E XI.

In order to prevent all Canfes of Complaint and Dispute which may arise on Account of Prizes which may be made at Sea after the Signature of the Preliminary Articles, it is reciprocally agreed that the Vessels and Effects which may be taken in the British Channel and in the North Seas, after the Space of Twelve Days, to be computed from the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Preliminary Articles, shall be redored on each Side; that the Term shall be One Month, from the British Channel and the North Seas, as far as the Canary Idands induftvely, whether in the Ocean or in the Mediterranean; Two Months, from the said Canary Islands as far as the Equator; and ladly. Five Months in all other Parts of the World, without any Exception, or any more particular Description of Time or Place.

ARTICLE XII.

All Sequedrations imposed by either of the Parties on the Funded Property, Revenues, or Debts, of any Description, belonging to either of the Contracting Powers, or to their Subjects or Citizens, shall be taken off immediately after the Signature of the Definitive Treaty. The Decision of all Claims brought forward by Individuals of the one Country against Individuals of the other, for private Rights, Debts, Property, or Effects whatsoever, which, according to received Usages and the Law of Nations, ought to revive at the Period of Peace, dull be heard and decided before the competent Tribunals; and in all Cases, prompt and

ample Justice shall be administered in the Countries where the Claims are made* It is agreed, moreover, that this Article, immediately after the Ratificatiofn of the Definitive Treaty, dull apply to the Allies of the Controlling Parties, and to the Individuals of the respective Nations, upon the Condition of a jud Reciprocity.

With respect to the Fisheries on the Coads of the Idand of Newfoundland, and of the Idands adjacent; and in the Gulph of Saint Lawrence, the Two Parties have agreed to redore them to the same Footing on which they were before the p'-efent War; reserving to themselves the Power of making in the Definitive Treaty, such Arrangements as shall appear jud and reciprocally useful, in order to place the Fishing of the Two Nations on the most proper Footing for the Maintenance of Peace.

ARTICLE XIV.

In all the Cafes of Reditution agreed upon by the present Treaty, the Fortifications shall be delivered up in the State in which they may be at the Time of the Signature of the present Treaty; and all the Works which shall have been conlhutted since the Occupation shall remain untouched.

It is farther agreed, that in all the Cafes of Cedion dipulated in the present Treaty, there shall be allowed to the Inhabitant, of whatever Condition or Nation they may be, a Term of Three Years, to be computed from the Notification of the Definitive Treaty of Peace, for the Purpose of disposing of their Properties acquired and possessed either before or during the present War; in the which Term of Three Years they may have the free fixer-cife of their Religion, and Enjoyment of their Property.

The same Privilege (half be granted in the Countries redored, to all those who shall have made therein any Edablishments whatsoever, during the Time when those Countries were in the Pose session of Great Britain.

With respect to the other Inhabitants of the Countries redored or ceded, it is agreed, that none of them shall be prosecuted, didurbed, or moleded, in their Persons or Properties, under any Pretext, on Account of their Conduct or Political Opinions, or of their Attachment to either of the Two Powers, nor on any other Account except that of Debts contracted to Individuals, or on Account of Alls poderior to the Definitive Treaty.

ARTICLE XV.

The present Preliminary Articles shall be ratified, and the Ratifications exchanged in London, in the Space of Fifteen Days, for all Delay; and immediately after their Ratification, Plenipoteiu tiaries shall be named, on each Side, who shall repair to Amiens for the Purpose of concluding a Definitive Treaty of Peace, im concert with the Allies of the Controlling Parties.

In Witness whereof, Wc, the undersigned Plenipotentiaries, of His Britannic Majesty, and of the Fird Consul of the French Republic, by virtue of our respective full Powers, have signed the present Preliminary Articles, and have caused our Seals to be put thereto.

Done at London the Fird Day of October One thousand Eight hundred and One, the Ninth Vendcmiaire, Year Ten of the French Republic.

(l. s.) Hawkesbury. (l. s.) Otto.

TRANSLATION of Treaty of Alliance between Hu MAjrsTY and the Ottoman Porte; signed at Con-stantinople, January 5th 1799.

In the Name of Almighty God !

THE constant and uninterrupted good Understanding which has ever subsisted between the August Court of London and the Sublime Ottoman Porte, as well as the Circumstances and Situation of the War in which the Two Sovereigns of the British and Ottoman Empires are engaged, in consequence of the perfidious and numerous Aggrefiions of the French, have inspired those Sovereigns with a mutual Desire to draw dill closer their ancient Bond of Friendship: And a Definitive Alliance having already been concluded between the Sublime Portp and his Majesty the Emperor of all the Rullias, the Friend and Ally of His Britannic Majesty, by which Alliance, founded on the Balls of 1 mutual Guarantee of their Empires, of the Re-establishment and Consolidation of general Tranquillity, and of the Preservation of the other Powers, it is agreed that His Britannic Majesty shall be invited to accede to it: Their said Majesties, namely, His Majesty George III. King of Great Britain, Arc. &c. Ac. and his Imperial Majesty Sultan Selim III. the Moll Mighty Ottoman Emperor, equally desirous of contributing to the Safety and to the Interelh of their respective Subjects, and to the Re-establishment of the general Tranquility of Europe, have, for these Purposes, named for their Plenipotentiaries; viz. the King of Great Britain, on His Part, Sir William Sidney Smith, Knight, Commander, Grand Cross of the Royal Military Order of the Sword, and Commodore of His Squadron actually in the Seas of the Levant, and John Spencer Smith, Esquire, His Minister Plenipotentiary actually residing at the Sublime Ottoman Porte; and his Imperial Majesty, on his Part, the Most Excellent and Moll Honourable EfTeid Ibrahim Ifmet Bev, distinguished by the Tit'e of Cazi AJker of Romilio, and formerly Cadi of Confiantinople, and Ahmed Aatif Reis Effendi, who, alter having reciprocally communicated their full Powers in good and due Form, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Article I. — His Biitannic Majesty, connected already with his Majesty the Emperor of Russia by the Ties of the strictest Alliance, accedes, by the present Treaty, to the Defenlive Alliance which has just been conclu led between his Majesty the 0‘toman Emperor and the Emperor of Russia, as far as the Stipulations thereof are applicable to the local Circumstances of his Empire, and of that of the Sublime Porte: And his Majesty the Ottoman Emperor enters reciprocally by U E Treaty into the same Engagements towards His Britannic Majesty, lo chat there shall exiil for ever between the Tlree Em; ire«, by virtue of the present Defensive Treaty, and of the Alliances and Treaties which already subsist. Peace, good Understanding, and perfect Friendship, as well by S a Land, so that for the future the Friends of One of the Parties Hull be the Friends of the Two others; and the Enemies of One shall, in like Manner, be considered as such by the others. On this Account the Two High Contracting Parties promise and engage to come to a frank and mutual Understanding in all Affairs in which their reciprocal Safety and Tranquillity may be interfiled, and to adopt, by common Confenr, the necessary Measures to oppose every Project hostile towards themselves, and to effectuate grneral Tranquillity.

II. — In older to give to this Alliance a full and entire Effect, the Two High Contracting Parties mutually guarantee to each other their PdLfnons; His Britannic Majesty guarantees all the Possessions of the Ottoman Empire, without Exception, such as they flood immediately before the Invasion of the French in Egypt: And his M ij'-fty the O:toman Emperor guarantees all the Poftcffions of Crc.it U it.iin, without ary Exception whatever.

Jii. — Notwithstanding the Two Contracting Parties reserve to themselves the full Right of cnteiing into Negociation with other Pwo, and to conclude with them whatever Treaties their In-tcrch mav require, yet they mutually bind themselves in the fin ngdl Manner, that inch Treaties shall not contain any Condition which can ever produce the lead Detriment, Injury, or Prejudice, to either of them, or aftcdl the Integrity of their Doming ns; on the contrary, they promise to regard and preserve, to their c:moil, their rec'prccal Honour, Safety, and Advantage.

IV. — In every same of an hostile Attack upon the Dominions of Cne of the Contracting Parti's the Succours wlvch the other is to fuitiifh shall be reg luted I v the Principles of good Faith, and in conVmity wb*i t' c ciufe Friendship subsisting between the Two E nj res, according to the Nature of the Cate.

V. — Whenever the Two Contracting Parties rn.,ke cominon Cause either with ad their Forces, or with th Succours furni'hed by virtue of this Alliance, neither Party Ilia* i'Mkc either Peace, ora durable Tiucc, without compiifing the o.her in it; tad without

flipulating for its Safety; and in case of an Attack against One of the Two Parties in hatred of the Stipulations of this Treaty, or of their faithful Execution, the other Party shall come to its Assistance in the Manner the most useful and the moil conformable to the common Interest, according to the Exigency of the Cafe.

VI. — The Two High Contracting Parties have agreed and resolved, that when their Fleets, Squad;ons, Ships, and other Vessels of War, shall meet, they shall salute each other. Attention being paid on both Sides, in order to begin the Salute, to the Superiority of Rank of the Commanders, manifelled by the Flag of Command; and in case of an Equality of Rank, no Salute shall be made. The Salute shall be answered by the same Number of Guns as were fired by the Party first saluting. Boats shall be reciprocally sent upon these Occasions for the Purpose of concerting the Mode of Salute, in order to avoid all Misunderstanding.

VII. — The Trophies, and all the Plunder taken from the Enemy, shall be the Property of the Troops making such Capture.

VIII. — The Two High Contracting Parties being actually engaged in War with the common Enemy, have agreed to make common Cause, and not to conclude any Peace or Truce but by common Consent, as it has been stipulated in the Fifth Article; (»> that on the one Side the Sublime Porte, notwithstanding the Cessation of the actual Attack directed against her Dominions, shall be bound to continue the War, and to remain attached to the Cause of her August Allies, until the Conclusion of a Peace just and honourable, as well for them as for herself; and, on the oilier Side, His Britannic Majesty shall be equally bound not to make Peace with the common Enemy without providing for the Intereils, the Honour, and the Safety of the Ottoman- Empire.

IX. — The Two Allies, making thus common Cause, promise to communicate to each other their Intentions re'ative to the Duration of the War, and to the Conditions of Peace, governing th?m-selves by juit and equitable Principles, and having an Understanding with each other in this respect.

X. — In order to render more efficacious the Succour to be furnished on both Sides during the War, according to the Spirit of the present Treaty of Alliance, the Two High Contracting Parties will concert together upon the Operations most suitable to be made in order to render abortive the pernicious Designs of the Enemy in general, and especially in Egypt, and to destroy their Commerce in the Seas of the Levant, and in the Mediterranean; and for this Purpose his Majesty the Ottoman Emperor engages not only to shut all his Ports, without Exception, against the Commerce of the Enemy, but likewise to employ against them in his Dominions (and in order to prevent the Execution of their ambitious ProjeCb) an Army, confiding at least of 100,000 Men, and even to augment it, in case of Need, to the Extent of his whole Forces: He shall also put his Naval Forces in a State of Preparation to act in concert with those of his Allies in the Seas above-mentionedAnd His Britannic Majesty, on His Parr, recipiocully engages Himself to employ in the same Seas, a Naval Force always equal to that of the Enemy, to annoy them; and to act in concert with the Fleets of LI is Allies, in order to impede the Execution of Their Plans, and especially to prevent any Attack upon the Dominions or Provinces of the Ottoman Empire.

XL — In as much as the Presence of the British Forces in the Seas of the Levant has for its principal Object the Defence of the Ottoman Coasts, and that Desertion, by weakening the Means, must unavoidably hurt the Cause, the Two High Contracting Powers promise not to tolerate it under 2ny Pretext or Motive.

XII. — notwithstanding the Tw o High Contracting Parties define to maintain these Engagements 11 Force as long as possible, nevertheless, as Circumstances might in Time require feme Change, it is agreed to fix the Term of Eight Years for this Definitive Treaty of Defensive Alliance, to be computed from the Day of the Ratifications being exchanged. At the Expiration of this Term, the Two Parties shall enter into amicable Explanations for the Renewal of it, conforming themselves to the then Situation of Affairs.

XIII. — The present Treaty of Defensive Alliance shall be ratified by His Majesty the Kng cf Great Britain, and his Majesty the Emperor of the Ottomans; and the Ratifications shall be exchanged at Confiantinople in Three Months, or so oner, ifpoftible.

In Witnesswhereof, We, undersigned Ministers Plenipotentiary aforesaid, have signed the present Treaty of Alliance; and have affixed to it the Seal of Our Arms, together with that of His Britannic Muji fly's Legation at the Sublime Ottoman Port.

Done at Confiantinople, the Fifth of January 1799.

(L.S.) JVm Sidney Smith. (L.S.) Ibrahim If meal Ley. (L.S.) J. Spencer Smith. (L.S.) Ahmed Aatif Rtis Yffouli.

1

In 1798 the Duty was lowered to £. 1. 171. 11 d. per Cwt.

From the many Regulations made at different Times of the Duties on TEAS Imported, various Rates having been at each Period laid on, according to the particular Value of " each Quantity, and the An* null Quantities Imported at each Description of Value never having been kept dif-tinct, it is impossible to ascertain the real Effect produced by every new Regulation. The Produce of Additional Duty is computed on this Principles vis. of a Comparative State* ment of what the Quantity at each New Duty would have produced, in proportion to the TotaJ Quantity and Duty of the preceding Years* Importation; which, deduced from the actual and known Produce under the New Rate, gives the-Increase of Duty.

The Three Amounts of Produce thus marked have been estimated; no particular Account of the Produce having been kept from the Period of their Consolidation; the First 10 per Cent, was Consolidated Section 1709, and the Second in Seinon 1800.

Copy of the DEFINITIVE TREATY of PE ACE between His Britannic Majesty and the French Republic, His Catholic Majesty, the Batavian Republic: Signed at Amiens the 27th Day of March 1802.

HIS MAJESTY the King of the U nfted Kingdom of G reat Britain and Ireland, and the First Consul of the French Republic, in the Name of the French People, being animated with an equal Desire to put an End to the Calamities of War, have laid the Foundation of Peace in the Preliminary Articles ligned at London the First of October One thousand Eight hundred and One (Ninth Venderaiaire, Year Ten :)

And as by the Fifteenth Article of the said Preliminaries it has been stipulated that Plenipotentiaries should be named on each Side, who should proceed to Amiens for the Purpose of concluding a Definitive Treaty, in concert with the Allies of the Contracting Powers;

His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland has named for His Plenipotentiary the Marquis Cornwallis, Knight of the Moll illuilrious Order of the Garter, Privy Counsellor to His Majesty, General of His Armies, &c.; the First Consul of the French Republic, in the Name of the French People, the Citizen Jtfeph Bonaparte, Counsellor of State; His Majesty the King of Spain and of the Indies, and the Government of the Batavian Republic, have named for their Plenipotentiaries, viz. H is Catholic Majesty, Don Joseph Nicolas de Azara, his Counsellor of State, Knight Great Cross of the Order of Charles III. his said Majesty's Ambassador Extraordinary to the French Republic, Sec.; and the Government of the Batavian Republic, Roger John Schimmelpenninck, their Ambassador Extraordinary to the French Republic; who, after having duly communicated to each other their full Powers, which are transcribed at the End of the present Treaty, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Article I. There shall be Peace, Friendship, and good Understanding, between His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, His Heirs and Successors, on the one Part; and the French Republic, his Majesty the King of Spain, his Heirs and Successors, and the Batavian Republic, on the other Part. The Contrafling Parties shall give the greatest Attention to maintain, between themselves and their States, a perfect Harmony, and without allowing on either Side any Kind of Hostilities, by Sea or by Land, to be committed for any Cause, or under any Pretence whatsoever.

They shall carefully avoid every thing which might hereafter affect the Union happily re-established, and they shall not afford any Aflillance or Protection, directly or indirectly, to those who should cause Prejudice to any of them.

Article II. All the Prisoners taken on either Side, as well by Land ay by Sea, and the Hostages carried away or given during the War, and to this Day, shall be restored without Ransom in Six Weeks at latest, to be computed from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty, and on paying the Debts which they have contracted during their Captivity. Each Con-trading Party shall respectively discharge the Advances which have been made by any of the Contracting Parties for the Subsistence and Maintenance of the Prisoners in the Country where they have been detained. For this Purpose a Commission shall be appointed by Agreement, which shall be specially charged to ascertain and regulate the Compenlaiion which may be due to either of the Contracting Powers. The Time and Place where the Commifuoncs, who shall be charged with the Execution of this Article, shall assemble, shall also be fixed upon by Agreement; and the said Commissioners shall take into Account the Expences occasioned, not only by the Prisoners of the respective Nations, hut also by the Foreign Troops, who, before they were made Pri-loners, were in the Pay, or at the Disposal, of any of the Con-trading Paitics.

Article III. His Britannic Majesty restores to the French Republic and her Allies, namely, his Catholic Majesty and the Batavian Republic, all the Poflc (lions and Colonies which belonged to them respectively, and which had been occupied or conquered by the British Forces in the Course of the War, with the Exception of the Island of Trinidad and the Dutch Possessions in the island of Ceylon.

Article IV. His Catholic Majesty cedes and guarantees, in full Right and Sovereignty, to His Britannic Majesty, the Island of 'Trinidad.

Article V.

SA MAJESTE le Roi du Rovaunie Uni de la Grande Bretagne ct d'lrlande, et le Premier Consul de la Republique Fran-9oise, au Nom du Peuple Francis, cgalement animes du Dcfir de faire cester les Calamitcs de la Guerre, ont pose les Fondemens de la Paix par les Articles Pr6Iinrinaires (igrt£s a Londres le Premier d'Odobre, Mil huit Cent Un (Neuf Vcndcmiaire, An Dix:)

Et comme par 1*Article Quinze des dits Preliminaires, il a etc convenu qu'il feroit nomme de Pan et d'autre des Plenipotentiaires qui fe rendroient & Amiens, pour y proceder & ia Redaction. du Trait£ Definkif, de concert avec les Allies des PttUlances Con* tradantes;

Sa Maje/16 le Roi du Royaume Uni de la Grande Bretagne et d'lrlande, a nomme le Marquis de Cornwallis, Chevalier de POrdre tres-iiluftre de la Jarreticrre, Conseiller Prive de Sa Majeste, General de Ses Arir.ees, Sec.; le Premier Consul de la Republique Fran9oise, au Nom du Peuple Franjoi*, le Crtoyrti Joseph Bonaparte, Confeilier d'Etat; fa Majeste le Roi tTEfpagne et des Indes et le Gouvemement d'Etat de Ia Republique Batave ont nommo pour leurs Plenipotentiaires, savoir, fa Majeste Catholique, Don Joseph Nicolas de Azara, son Conseiller d'Etat, Chevalier Grand Croix de TOrdre de Charles HI. Ambafladcur Extraordinaire de fa dite Majeste pres la Republique Fran^ife, Sec. et le Gouverne-ment d'Etat de la Republique Batave, Roger Jean Schimmelpenninck, son Ambafladeur Extraordinaire pies la Republique Fran-9oise, ldquels apres s'etre duement communiques leurs pleins Pouvoirs, qui font transerits a la Suite du present Traite, (ont convenus des Articles fuivans:

Article I. SEPARATE ARTICLE.

It is agreed. That the Omission of some Titles, which may have taken place in the present Treaty, shall not be prejudicial to the Powers or to the IVrlocis concerned.

It is farther agreed, that the English and French Languages made use of in all the Copies of the present Treaty shall not form an Example which may be alledged or quoted as a Precedent, or in any Manner prejudice the Contracting Powers whose Languages have not been used; and that for the future what has been observed, and ought to be observed, with regard to, and on the Part of Powers who are in the Practice and Possession of giving and receiving Copies of like Treaties in any other Language, shall be conformed with; the present Treaty having, nevertheless, the same Force and Virtue as if the aforesaid Practice had been therein observed.

In Witness whereof. We, the underwritten Plenipotentiaries of His Britannic Majesty, of the French Republic, of his Catholic Majesty, and of the Batavian Republic, have signed the present Separate Article, and have caused our respective Seals to be affixed thereto.

TransUtion of a TREATY between his Catholic Majesty and the Prince Regent of Portugal;

signed at Badajoz, June 6th, 1801.

Appendix, (No. 72.,) 11# Mali.

THE End being obtained which his Catholic Majesty pfoposed to himself, and judged necessary for the general Good of Europe, at the Time of his declaring War again# Portugal; and the Belligerent Powers having mutually combined with his said Majesty;

They have determined to establish, and renew the Conne&iona of Amity and good Correspondence, by means of a Treaty of Peace.

The Plenipotentiaries of the Three Belligerent Powers have met, and agreed upon the forming Two Treaties (these being only One in the essential Part, as the Guarantee is reciprocal); neither of the Two to have any Validity, should an Infraction of any of the Articles contained therein be proved.

In order then to obtain so important an Object, his Royal Highness the Prince Regent of Portugal and of the Algarves, and his Catholic Majesty the King of Spain, have granted their full Powers to negotiate as followsHis Royal Highness the Prince Regent of Portugal and of the Algarves, to his Excellency Luiz Pinto de Souza Continho, one of his Counsellors of State, &c.&c.&c.; and his Catholic Majesty the King of Spain, to his Excellency Don Manfel de Godoy Alfarez de Faria Rios Sanches e Sargofa, Prince of Peace, Sec. See. Sec Who, after having communicated to each other their full Powers, and found them drawn up in proper and regular Form, have agreed upon, and confirmed the following Articles, regulated by the Orders and Instructions of their respective Sovereigns:

Article I. Peace, Friendrtup, and good Intercourse, shall subsist between His Royal Highness the Prince Regent of Portugal and the Algarves, and his Catholic Majesty the King of Spain, both by Sea and Land, throughout the whole Extent of their Dominions; and all Prizes made by Sea, after the Ratification of the present Treaty, shall be faithfully restored; together with all Sorts of Merchandize and Goods, or their respective Value.

Article II. His Royal Highness shall (hut up the Ports of all his Dominions to the Vessels of Great Britain, in general.

Article III. His Catholic Majesty shall restore to his Royal Highness the Fortresses and Places of Icromenha, Arronches, Portalegre, Caftello de Vide, Barbacena Campo Mayor, and Onguello, with all his Territories, either conquered already, or which may be conquered; together with all the Artillery, Muskets, and other Ammunition found in the said Fortresses and Places, which shall be restored in the same Condition as they were in at the Time of their being surrendered. His said Majesty shall retain in quality of Conquetl, and unite for ever to his Dominions and Subjects, the Post of Oliven^a, its Territory and Inhabitants, from the Guadiana, so that this River may be the Limit of the respective Kingdoms in that Part which touches the above-mentioned Territory of Olivenfa only.

Article IV. His Royal Highness the Prince Regent of Portugal and the Algarves, shall not permit, on the Frontiers of his Kingdoms, Depots of prohibited and contraband Effects, which may prejudice the Commerce and Interests of the Crown of Spain, beyond such as may exclusively belong to the Regal Revenue of the Crown of Portugal, and be necessary to the Consumption of the respective Territories in which they are madeshould this, or any other Article be infringed, the Treaty now establishing between the Three Powers is to be considered as void.

Article V. His Royal Highness shall, without Delay, make good to the Subjects of his Catholic Majesty, when jijftly claimed, all Losses caused by the Armaments of Great Britain, or the Subjects of the Crown of Portugal, during the War with either of these Powers; in like Manner, his Catholic Majesty will give just Satisfaction to his Royal Highness on the Subject of all Captures made illegally by the Spaniards, before the War now existing, by Infraction of Territory, or within Cannon-(hot of the Portuguese Fortrefle?.

Article VI. Before the Expiration of Three Months from the Ratification of the present Treaty, his Royal Highness shall pay ' into his Catholic Majesty^ Treasury, the Expences (which his

Vol. 57.

Troops neglected satisfying when they withdrew from the French War) according to the Statement already given in by his said Majesty *3 Ambassador, or which may again be given in; Errors in the above-mentioned Statements excepted.

Article VII. Immediately on the Confirmation of the present Treaty, Hostilities shall reciprocally cease within the precise Space of Twenty Hours; after this Term, no Contributions, or other Exadions whatever, shall be demanded of the conquered People, farther than what is usually granted to friendly Troops in Time of Peace. And upon the Ratification of the said Treaty, the Spanish Troops shall evacuate the Portuguese Territory within the exact Limit of Six Days, beginning to march Twenty-four Hours from its being notified to them. They shall commit no Acts of Violence or Exadion as they pass along, but shall pay for whatever they want, according to the Market Price of the Country.

Article VIII. All Prisoners made by Sea and Land shall be immediately set at Liberty, and mutually restored, within Fifteen Days after ratifying the present Treaty, upon paying all Debts which may have been contracted during their Detention.

The Sick and Wounded shall continue to be taken Care of in their respective Hospitals, and shall be also given up whenever they are able to March.

Article IX. His Catholic Majesty binds himself to guarantee to his Royal Highness the Prince Regent of Portugal, the intire Preservation of his States and Dominions, without the slighted Exception or Reserve.

Article X. The Two high contracting Powers oblige themselves to renew immediately the Treaties of Defenflve Alliance which subsisted between the Two Monarchies, with such Clauses and Modifications however as are required by the Connedions which at present unite the Spanish Monarchy to the French Republic; in the same Treaty they must also regulate the Assistance which is to be mutually^fcnc, whenever any Exigence may require it.

Article XI. The present Treaty shall be ratified within the exact Space of Ten Days after being mutually agreed upon, or before, if possible.

In Faith of which. We, the underwritten Ministers Plenipotentiary, sign, in the Name of our August Masters, and in virtue of our full Powers with which they have inverted ua for that Purpose, the present Treaty, and have sealed it with the Seal of our Arms.

Done in the City of Badajoz, June 6th, 1801.

Luiz Pinto de Souza. (l. s.)

El Princejfe de la Paz. (l. s. )

Translation of a TREATY of PEACE between the French Republic and the Kingdom of Portugal; signed at Madrid the 9th Vendemiaire, Year Ten (39th September 1801.)

THE First Consul of the French Republic, in the Name of the French People, and His Royal Highness the Prince Regent of the Kingdom of Portugal, and of the Algarves, equally animated with the Desire of re-establishing those Relations of Commerce and Amity which subsisted between both States previous to the present War, have determined to conclude a Treaty of Peace, through the Mediation of his Catholic Majesty, and have appointed (or this Purpose the following Plenipotentiaries; Viz.

The First Consul of the French Republic, in the Name of the French People, Citizen Lucien Bonaparte, and his Royal Highness the Prince Regent of the Kingdom of Portugal and of the Algarves, his Excellency Cypriano Ribiero Freire, Commander of the Order of Christ, one of the Council of bu Royal Highness,

and

Appendix, (No. 72.)

11* Alaiit

and his Minider Plenipotentiary to his Catholic Majesty; which Plenipotentiaries after having exchanged their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles:

entinutd. Article I. There shall be henceforth, and for ever. Peace,

— ..J Friendship, and good Undemanding, between the French Republic

and the Kingdom of Portugal. All Hostilities, both by Land and ' Sea, shall cease after the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty; that is to say: Within Fifteen Days in Europe and the Seas which bound it, and the Coast of Africa, on this Side of the Equator; within Forty Days after the said Exchange in the Countries and Seas of America and Africa beyond the Equator; and Three Months after it in the Countries and Seas to the Westward of Cape Horn, and to the East of the Cape of Good Hope. All the Prizes made after each of these Periods, in the Latitudes mentioned, shall be respectively restored. The Prisoners of War on each Side shall be redored, and the same political Relations re-established between the Two Powers as cxitled before the War,

Article II. All the Ports and Roads of Portugal in Europe shall be immediately (hut, and continue so until the Conclusion of Peace between France and England, against all English Ships of War and Merchantmen; and the said Ports and Roads shall be open to all the Ships of War and Merchantmen belonging to the French Republic and her Allies. As to the Ports and Roads of Portugal in other Parts of the World, the present Article shall be obligatory within the Periods above fixed for the Ceffacion of I loflilitics.

Article III. Portugal engages not to furnish, during the Course of the present War, to the Enemies of the French Republic and her Allies, any Succours in Troops, Vessels, Arms, Warlike Stores, Provisions, or Money of any Kind, or in any Manner whatever. All anterior Acts, Engagements, or Conventions, contrary to the present Article, are hereby revoked, and regarded as null and void.

The Indians of the Two Guianas, who in the course of the War may hare been carried off from their Habitations, shall be respectively redored. The Citizens or Subjects of the Two Powers, who may be comprized within the new Determination of the Limits, may reciprocally retire to the Posse (lions of their respective States. They shall likewise have Power to dispose of their Property, moveable and immoveable, during a Period of Two Years, to be computed from the Day of exchanging the Ratifications of the present Treaty.

Article V. A Treaty of Commerce and Navigation shall be negociated between the Two Powers which shall definitively settle the Commercial Relations between France and Portugal: in the mean time it is agreed,

1. That the Communication shall be re-established immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications, and that the Agents and Factors of Commerce shall, on each Side, be restored to the Possession of the Rights, Immunities, and Prerogatives, which they enjoyed before the War.

ad. That the Citizens and Subjects of the Two Powers shall equally and reciprocally enjoy in the States of either, all the Rights therein enjoyed by those of the most favoured Nations.

3d. That the Commodities and Merchandize produced from the Soil or Manufactures of each of the Two Powers shall be admitted reciprocally, without Restriction, and without being liable to any Duty which would not equally affect the Commodities and Merchandize of a similar Nature imported by other Nations.

4th. That the French Cloths may be immediately imported into Portugal on the Footing of the most favoured Merchandize.

Jth. That in other Points all the Stipulations relative to Trade, inserted in preceding Treaties, and not contrary to the present Treaty, shall be provisionally executed until the Conclusion of a definitive Treaty of Commerce.

Article VI. The Ratifications of the present Treaty of Peace shall be exchanged at Madrid, in the Term of Twenty Days at farthed.

Article IV. The Boundaries of French and Portuguese Guiana shall be determined in future by the River Carapanatuba, which falls into the River Amazon, at about a Third of a Degree of North Latitude from the Equator above Fort Macapa. These Limits shall follow the Course of the River to its Source, from whence they shall take a Direction towards the Grand Chain of Mountains which divide the Course of the River; they shall follow the Windings of that Chain to the Point neared to Rio Branco, about Two and a Third Degrees North of the Equator.

Done at Madrid (a Duplicate being at the same Time executed) the 7th Vende-miaire. Year Ten of the French Republic (le 29 Sepr 1801.

(Signed) Lucien Bonaparte.

Cypriano Ribiero Freire.

Translation of ADDITIONAL ARTICLES, signed at Moscow, the y* October 1801, to the Convention, between His Majesty and the Emperor of Russia; concluded at St. Petersburgh, the y June 1801.

WHEREAS by the 6th Article of the Convention, concluded the y June 1801, between His Briunnick Majesty and his Imperial Majesty of all the Ruflias, it was stipulated, that the Two High Contracting Parties should mutually agree on some Additional Articles, which should fix the Regulations and Principles to be observed, as well for accelerating the judicial Proceedings upon Captures made at Sea, as for the Damages which should be allowed to the Owners of Neutral Ships and Cargoes, in Cafes of unfounded Detention, Their said Majesties have named and authorized for this Purpose, viz. His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, Alleyne Lord Baron St. Helen's, a Peer of the said United Kingdom, one of His said Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council, and His Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to his Majesty the Emperor of all the Ruflias; and his Majesty the Emperor of all the Ruflias, the Sieur Alexander Prince de Kourakin, his Vice Chancellor, Actual Counsellor, Mi-nider of the Council of State, Actual Chamberlain, Grand Chancellor of the Sovereign Order of St. John of Jerusalem, and Knight of the Russian Orders of St. Andrew, of St. Alexander New(ky, and of St. Anne of the First CIafs; of those of Prussia, of the Black and Red Eagles; of those of Denmark, of the Danebrog, and of the Perfect Union; and Grand Crofsof the Sovereign Order of St. John of Jerusalem: and the Sieur Victor Count de Kotfchoubey, his Actual Privy Counsellor, Minister for the Department for Foreign A (Fairs, Senator, A dual Chamberlain, and Knight of the Orders of St. Alexander Newlky of St. Vladimir of the Second

Class, and Commander of the Sovereign Order of St. John of Jerusalem; who, in virtue of their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Article I. In case of unfounded Detention or other Contravention of the edab'ished Regulations, the Owners of the Vessel and Cargo so detained shall be allowed Compensation for each Day's Demurrage, proportionate to the Loss they shall have fudained, according to the Freight of the Taid Ship, and the Nature of its Cargo.

Article II. If the Miniders of one of the High Contracting Parties, or any other Persons accredited by the same to the Belligerent Power, should remonstrate against the Sentence which shall have been passed by the respective Courts of Admiralty upon the said Captures, Appeal shall be made, in Rudia, to the directing Senate, and, in Great Britain, to His Majesty's Privy Council.

Article III. Care shall be taken on both Sides scrupulously to examine whether the Regulations and Precautions agreed upon in the present Convention have been observed, which shall be done with all possible Dispatch. The Two high Contracting Parties moreover mutually engage to adopt the most efficacious Measures, in order to prevent the Sentences of their several Tribunals respecting Captures made at Sea being subject to any unnecessary Delay.

Article

Article IV. The Goods in Litigation cannot be fold or an* loaded before final Judgment, without an argent and real Necessity, which shall have been proved before the Court of Admiralty, and by virtue of a Commission to this Effect; and the Captort Hull by no means be permitted to remove or take away, on their own Authority, either opemy or clandestinely, any thing from a Vessel so detained.

These Additional Articlei, making Part of the Convention signed the V June 1801, in the Names of their Britannidc and Imperial Majesties, shall have the same Force and Validity as if they were inserted Word for Word in the said Convention.

In Witness whereof. We, the Undersigned, furnished with the full Powers of their said Majesties, have signed in their Names the p efent Additional Articles, and have affixed the Seal of our Arms thereto.

Venereal

Venereal Difeafr*, and is the only Institution in the Kingdom of Ireland exclusively appropriated to the Relief of Persons of that Drfcription: It i> therefore refored to by infe^ed Persons from all Parts of the Kingdom, Sailors belonging to different Nations, and Soldiers ditchai grd from His Majesty's Service. The Hospital is capable of accommodating only Two Hundred and Fifty Intern Patients, and is uudequ te to the Reception of the Number applying for Relief.

The S enior and Aflidant Surgeons attend every Day at Twelve o'Clock to vif:t the Wards, to dispence Medicine to Extern Patients, and to confuit upon any same of Danger or Emergency; the Senior Surgeons also attend twice a Week to adapt and distribute Truffes to the Ruptured Poor.

The Senior Su g^ons report, that in their Opinion the Building, as it now (lands, is sufficiently spacious to contain the Patients under Mercurial Treatment; but that in order to carry the Intentions of Government completely into Effect, it will be expedient to ertft Two spauous and ventilated Wards (apart from the Mercurial Wards) for the Accommodation of Convalescents, or Patients to whom Mercury Cannot with Propriety be administered, capable of containing Twenty-five Beds each.

iY?/*. — In the Year 1697, certain Rates of Value were affixed to the several Articles Imported into and Exported from this Kingdom; and consonant to these Estimates, the Ledgers of the Inspector General's Office are still kept, and the Accounts are Rated accordingly.

Under the Act of the 38th of His Majesty, commonly called The Convoy A ft, N the Merchants Exporters were required to declare the Real Value of British Manufactures Exported, in order that the Amount of the Duty chargeable thereon might be ascertained; bat the Act having expired on the ifl Day of lall October, and the Exporters being confcauently exempt from their Declaration as to the Value, the Inspector General cannot make an Official Return to that Part of the Order of the House, which requires the Difference between the Official Value, and the Declared Value, in the Year ending the 5th January 1802. Assuming however, that Articles Exported subsequent to the jft of October, may be cflimated at the same Rate of Value with Articles of a similar Nature, Exported in the preceding Period of the Year, when the true Valqe could be ascertained by the Declaration of the Exporters; the Inspector General thinks himself justified in Rating to Parliament, That <r the Actual Value of " British Manufactures Exported from Great Britain to all Parts, amounted, in the Year 1801, to £.41,770,354.99

No Account can as yet be prepared of the Value of the Imports from India and China, for the Year ending the 5th January last.

Inspector General's Office, Custom-House, London, 14th May 1802.

William Irving,

Inspector General of the Imports and Exports of Great Britain.

The Returns from many of the Ports in the Plantations being unreceived, and others which are received Banding in Need of Correction, that Part of this Account which relates to the Year 1801, is from that Cause unavoidably defective; but I conceive that the Defect is not equal to the Amount of Shipping belonging to those Ports, because it always happens, that when the Returns from all the Ports in the British Empire are collected together, and checked by each other, some Alterations become necessary in most of them, owing to the Circumstance of Vessels being registered de novo at Ports to which they did not formerly belong, without the Knowledge of the Officers at such former Ports; I therefore do not presume to lay this Account before the House, as correct with respect to that Year.

May 15 th, 1802. Jm Dalley,

In the Year 1801, there has been an Increase of Four in the Number, and of £. 1,960. in the Annual Amount of the Salaries of the Officers of His Majesty's Secretary at War (including retired Officers) in the Manner following:

Per Annum.

The Chief Examiner of Army Accompts, on account of his extreme ill Health from a Paralytic Stroke (after a Service of more than 35 Years) was permitted to retire on an Allowance for his Life of £. 1,100 per Annum, to commence from Christmas 1801 [up to which Time his full Salary of £. 1,500 was continued to him] - - - £. 1,100

The Salaries of several Clerks have been augmented, in consequence of Increase of Business and Responsibility, or, from the PrefTure of the Times; viz.

One Principal Clerk, who ceased to act, and receive Salary as Private Secretary to the Secretary at War, from £.1,000 to £.1,100 ——

One, who has been nearly 25 Years in the Office, from £.900 to £*950 - -

One Clerk for MiLellaneous Accompts, not on the Establishment of the Office, from £.200 to £.300....

LOTTERY OFFICE.

SIR,

In Obedience to the Order of the House of Commons, communicated to the Commissioners of the Lottery by your Letter of the ad of this Month, I am directed by them to inform you, that the Expences in this Office are not reckoned by Years, but by Lotteries, which run from one Year into another.

Lottery i8ci, is now in the course of Drawing at Guildhall; and the Accounts of it will not be finifoed till the Year following.

The Establishment of the Lottery 1800 is, in respect to the Number of Commissioners, of Officers, and of Clerics, precisely the same that of the Lottery 1796, delivered to the Financial Committee of the House of Commons in 1798; and their Appointments are the fame; but there is a Diminution in the General Expence of the Lottery 1800, of about Ninety-three Pounds.

No Emoluments accrue to the Managers besides their Salaries, excepting a Charge for Entertainment and Coach-hire, as afual, to those who are upon Duty at Guildhall. But the Officers and Four Senior Clerks on the Establishment, divide some Fees arising chiefly from the Dciirc of Adventurers to know the Fate of their Tickets, for the Examination of each of which Sixpence is paid.

I remain. Sir,

Your mott obedient and mott humble Servant,

Lottery Office, 7 Gray.

V. — The Amount of Land Tax redeemed, or to be redeemed,

by virtue of such Sales, and Contract for Sale, cannot yet be dated with Precifion, as in several Indances, the Money anting from Sales approved and confirmed by the Lords Commissioners, has not yet been paid into the Bank.

Besides which, the Property sold by the Corporate Bodies, being required by Law to be sold free and discharged from Land Tax, the Land Tax has in very many Cafes, by Agreement between the Parties, been freed by the Lessee tr Purchaser at his Expence.

It is therefore difficult to ascertain what Amount of Land Tax may have been redeemed by this Part of the Operation.

On the Whole, however, the Amount of Land Tax redeemed by virtue of the aforesaid Sales and Contrails for Sale, may be cltimated at ,£.35.000 per Annum.

X. — The Value of the entire Property, of which the Tenure has been changed by the Ed eel of the Sales, and Contrails for Sale, has been computed to be not less than Thiee Times the Amount of the whole Sum received. AfTuming this Computation to be well founded, the Amount fold or contracted for being £.753,834, the Value in Tec of the whole Property transferred from Corporate bodies, will be £. 2,261,502.

The Prices approved in Sales, and Contrails for Sale, have varied from 6 to 9 Years Pure hale, for the Reversion in Fee of Linds and Tythes under Leases lor Three Lives; from 8 to 14 Years.Purchase for the Reversion in Fee of Leases for 21 Years 5 Years Purchase has been taken for Houses let for 30 Years, and 3 Years for the Reversion in Fee of Leases for 40 Years; reserved Rents, and Property not let on bencticial Leases, have been fold from 25 to 30 Years Purchase.

XI. — There cannot be a Doubt that these Sales are.convenicnr to Purchasers, advantageous to the Sellers, and their Successors, and highly beneficial to the Public in general: And therefore the Lords Commissioners would gladly have added to this Report, some Eilimate of the Proportion of Land Tax payable, and not yet redeemed, by the Bodies Corporate.

It is, however, difficult to arrive at any Certainty in this Part of the Enquiry. It is probable that the Proportion of Land Tax redeemed by the Corporate Bodiet and the r Leflles, may exceed the Proportion as yet redeemed by other Dcfcitpiions of Property chargeable with Land Tax; Hill, however, it may be estimated that more than Two-Thirds remain unredeemed.

VI. — The Quantity of Stock purchased by the Bank from the Produce of such Sales, is £. 1,013,000; exclusive of the Sums not paid into the Bank, and also of Sums not yet brought to Account, amuunting together by Eilimate to £. 200,000 Stock.

VII. — The Gain resulting to the Public from the Proceedings under the Commission, confiAs, molV immediately, in the On«-Klcventh required by the A^lj, to be paid to the Public, beyond the Value of the Land Tax redeemed, and such Gain cannot be Hated at less than £. 110,000 Stock; and this is exclusive of the Land Tax redeemed by the Lessees and Purchasers of many considerable Parcels of the Property sold to them. A further Gain resulting to the Public from the Proceedings under the Commission, U to be found in the general Operation of the Redemption of the Land Tax, particularly by creating a daily Demand of a certain Proportion of Stock, which can never be brought back into the Market.

XII. — The general Results may be stated to be: —

That the Number of Sales approved is 1,605.

That the Amount in Money of such Sales so approved, is £ 753>S34 Sterling.

That the Value in Fee Simple of the Property fold, is above £. 2,coc, oco Sterling.

That the Stock purchased for the Redemption of Land Tax, under the Proceedings of the Commissioners, is about £. »,200,000.

That the whole Expence to the Public his been £. 5,400.

That the Gain to the Public, by the Operation, Ins not been less than £. m0,000 Stock; exclusive of the other Benefits explained and detailed in this Report.

By Order of the Lords Commissioners,

/r. Young,
